text:
Exolum has commenced operations at the aviation fuel storage and distribution facilities and the hydrant network at Cristiano Ronaldo International Airport in Madeira, Portugal, managed by ANA (VINCI Group).

The company will invest more than €4.5 million by 2029 in the construction of new infrastructure designed to increase the facility’s storage capacity to 1,300 m³. The contract has an initial term of seven years, with the option to extend to nine years.

The scope of the project includes the comprehensive operation of the fuel storage facility (fuel farm), currently comprising six horizontal tanks, as well as the hydrant system, which is over one kilometre long and has 32 supply points. Furthermore, Exolum will lead the design and implementation of new infrastructure aimed at increasing storage capacity and improving the facility’s operational efficiency.

The project will be carried out in several phases and will include the construction of new tanks, the progressive modernisation of existing facilities and the implementation of advanced control and safety systems. This investment will increase the airport’s operational autonomy to five days and will also facilitate the implementation of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) in Madeira.

Javier Goñi, CEO of Exolum: “With the addition of Madeira Airport, we are now present at 50 airports, guaranteeing a reliable, efficient supply that meets the highest quality standards. This presence provides us with extensive knowledge and solid experience in airport management across Europe and the Americas. Aviation is a strategic area for our company in which we want to continue growing.”

Madeira’s Cristiano Ronaldo International Airport handles over 5 million passengers a year. With more than 600 weekly flights, it is one of Portugal’s busiest airports and a leading global tourist destination. The most recent forecasts estimate that by 2030 it will supply an annual average of 120,000 m³ of fuel, compared to 105,000 m³ distributed in 2025.

In Portugal, Exolum also operates Lisbon’s Humberto Delgado Airport, which in 2025 exceeded 36 million passengers.

Rui Coutinho, Madeira Airport Director, commented: “At ANA | VINCI Airports, as operators of critical infrastructure, we have a responsibility to ensure the reliability, efficiency, and long-term capacity of our facilities. This investment at Madeira Airport is a clear example of that commitment, reinforcing fuel infrastructure to support the airport’s continued growth while maintaining the highest standards of safety and operational performance.”

title: הפיילוט יוצא לדרך: השאריות של משחטת העוף יזרמו למנוע של מטוס הסילון - TheMarker
description:
תחליף הנפט הזה מיועד להגיע לבתי הזיקוק, שם הוא ישמש בעיקר לייצור דלק מטוסים בר־קיימא (Sustainable Aviation Fuel, או SAF).
"חברות תעופה נדרשות כיום למצוא פתרונות לדלק נקי, ולרגולציה הזאת יש השפעה רוחבית על העולם כולו", מסביר מנבר.
לא תלויים בשרשרת האספקה הבינלאומית לפי דו"ח סוכנות האנרגיה הבינלאומית (IEA), פליטות גזי החממה ממגזר התעופה הן כ–2.5% מסך הפליטות הגלובליות — נתח שיהיה קשה לצמצם.
במסגרת הפיילוט, כ–100 טונה של שומן בחודש אמורות להפוך לשמן המתאים לזיקוק לדלק סילוני — כמות שוות ערך לכ–730 חביות נפט.
"כדי למהול את כל הדלק הסילוני בישראל לרמה של 2% SAF, נדרשות 60–70 טונה של חומר גלם ביום.
text:
בפינה מרוחקת של משחטת עוף הנגב, בסמוך לעיר אופקים, עומדת מכולה שדפנותיה הוסרו. בקצה האחד שלה מותקן משפך מתכת ענק, ובקצה השני — צינור שממנו אמור לזרום תחליף לנפט. בתוך מסגרת המכולה מותקנת שורה של מכלים וצינורות. זהו המתקן המסחרי הראשון מסוגו שהקימה חברת נקי (NAKI), לאחר עשרות הרצות מוצלחות במעבדה.

ביקרתי במקום במהלך סיור של קהילת החדשנות באנרגיה Ignite The Spark, שעסק בתעשיית האנרגיה בנגב המערבי. עוד לפני שעלינו לאוטובוס במתקן של חברת תש"א (תשתיות אנרגיה) הלאומית, הכין אותנו המייסד והמנכ"ל, ברק מנבר, לריח העז שאנחנו צפויים לו. ואכן, כמה מהמשתתפים שירדו מהאוטובוס מיהרו לחזור אליו כעבור דקות ספורות, עוד לפני שהחל ההסבר.

"התחליף שאנחנו מייצרים פה יכול להחליף את הנפט הגולמי בבתי הזיקוק מבלי שהם יידרשו לבצע התאמה כלשהי במתקנים שלהם", מסביר מנבר, שייסד את החברה יחד עם מיכאל קופליק, המכהן כ–CTO. בנקי פיתחו טכנולוגיה שמאפשרת להפיק מפסולת אורגנית שמן המשמש תחליף לנפט, שאותו הם מכנים Mida Oil. במקום שהפסולת מהמשחטה תופנה להטמנה, היא נהפכת למשאב בעל ערך כלכלי. תחליף הנפט הזה מיועד להגיע לבתי הזיקוק, שם הוא ישמש בעיקר לייצור דלק מטוסים בר־קיימא (Sustainable Aviation Fuel, או SAF).

נקי מבקשת לתת מענה לרגולציה העולמית שמחמירה והולכת, ובראשה זו של האיחוד האירופי. החל מ–2030, כל מטוס שינחת בנמל התעופה של האיחוד יחויב להשתמש בתמהיל דלק המכיל SAF — תחילה אחוזים בודדים ממנו (2%), אך השיעור יעלה בהדרגה. חברות תעופה שלא יעמדו בתקנה יידרשו לשלם מסים גבוהים יותר.

"חברות תעופה נדרשות כיום למצוא פתרונות לדלק נקי, ולרגולציה הזאת יש השפעה רוחבית על העולם כולו", מסביר מנבר. "השאיפה היא להביא את עולם התעופה לאפס פליטות עד 2050. לפי ההערכות, המשמעות היא שהעולם יידרש לכ–450 מיליון טונה של דלק מטוסים בר קיימא בשנה", הוסיף.

לא תלויים בשרשרת האספקה הבינלאומית

לפי דו"ח סוכנות האנרגיה הבינלאומית (IEA), פליטות גזי החממה ממגזר התעופה הן כ–2.5% מסך הפליטות הגלובליות — נתח שיהיה קשה לצמצם. בעוד בענפי תחבורה אחרים המבוססים על דלקים — כמו רכבים פרטיים — יש פתרונות חשמליים זמינים, למטוסים מסחריים גדולים אין כרגע חלופה חשמלית ריאלית. לכן, המענה המרכזי הוא החלפת הדלק הסילוני המזוקק מנפט בדלק בר קיימא ממקורות חלופיים.

אחד האתגרים המרכזיים בייצור SAF הוא מציאת חומרי גלם זמינים בכמויות מספקות, שאינם מתחרים בגידולי חקלאות למזון או דורשים שימושי קרקע נרחבים (כמו גידול סויה לדלק). כאן נכנסות שאריות העוף של משחטת עוף הנגב.

המתקן נמצא בימים אלה לקראת תחילתו של פיילוט, שבמסגרתו הוא אמור לטפל בכ–700 טונה של פסולת (בוצה) בחודש. לפני שהשאריות מגיעות למתקן של נקי, מפעל עוף הנגב מפריד מהן את הפסולת המימית; המים מופנים למתקן טיהור השפכים הצמוד למשחטה, ושאר הבוצה המרוכזת מועברת אל מכולת הטיפול.

"אנחנו יושבים בין שתי תעשיות שכל אחת מהן מזהמת בדרכה, ומצליחים להפוך את שתיהן לקצת יותר ירוקות", אומר מנבר. "בסופו של דבר העולם עדיין תלוי בנפט, והשאלה היא אם נוכל לעזור לו להיות מעט יותר נקי. המוצר שלנו הוא נפט שלא מביא איתו את התלות בשרשרת אספקה בינלאומית מורכבת — הוא מיוצר מקומית, באתר עצמו. וזה לא משנה אם מפיקים אותו במשחטה, במפעל גלידה או במפעל שמייצר אוכל מוכן".

להרוויח משני הקצוות

כיום, מפעלים משלמים 150–400 שקל עבור פינוי והטמנה של כל טונת פסולת (בהתאם לסוג הפסולת ולמרחק הפינוי). נקי לוקחת את הפסולת הזאת ומציעה להם פתרון קצה מקומי ומשתלם יותר בתוך המפעל.

"אנחנו מבצעים פירוק של חלבונים ושומנים באמצעות חומרים כימיים שפועלים במערכת סגורה", מפרט מנבר. "החלבונים, שהם כ–80% מהבוצה, מופנים למתקני ביו־גז לייצור חשמל. השומנים, שהם ה–20% הנותרים, מיועדים לבתי הזיקוק".

במסגרת הפיילוט, כ–100 טונה של שומן בחודש אמורות להפוך לשמן המתאים לזיקוק לדלק סילוני — כמות שוות ערך לכ–730 חביות נפט. לשם ההשוואה, ובאופן תיאורטי, כמות השמן שייצר המתקן במשך שנה שלמה תוכל לספק את תפוקת הזיקוק של בית הזיקוק בחיפה (בז"ן) למשך שעה בודדת. ברור שאלה אינן כמויות שישנו לבדן את מפת האנרגיה, אך המטרה אינה להחליף את כל הנפט הגולמי, אלא לספק בשלב הראשון את אותם 2% של רכיב ירוק הדרושים כדי לעמוד ברגולציה האירופית.

"בדקנו את השוק המקומי", מסביר מנבר. "כדי למהול את כל הדלק הסילוני בישראל לרמה של 2% SAF, נדרשות 60–70 טונה של חומר גלם ביום. לשם כך אנחנו צריכים להציב כ–40 מתקנים כאלה במפעלים שונים ברחבי ישראל".

המודל העסקי של נקי בנוי על הכנסה כפולה: החברה גם מציבה את המתקן במפעל ומקבלת תשלום על עצם פינוי והפחתת הפסולת, וגם מוכרת את תחליף הנפט האיכותי לבתי הזיקוק.

להערכת החברה, עלות הייצור של חבית שמן כזאת תהיה כ–35 דולר בלבד, וכל מתקן שיוקם צפוי להחזיר את ההשקעה בו בתוך כשנתיים וחצי. חלק מהיכולת להפחית בצורה דרמטית את עלויות הייצור נובע מהסימביוזה התעשייתית: נקי מנצלת את עודפי החום והקור של מפעל המזון כדי לחסוך באנרגיה הדרושה לתהליך הייצור.

"החזון שלנו הוא לשנות מן היסוד את הדרך שבה התעשייה העולמית מתייחסת לפסולת שלה", מסכם מנבר. "במקום לקבור אותה באדמה ולשלם על כך, אפשר להפוך אותה לדלק ירוק בייצור מקומי, ולקחת חלק במעבר הגלובלי לאנרגיה נקייה יותר".

title: Worley Completes FEED for Alfanar Lighthouse Green Fuels SAF Project in Teesside
description:
Worley has completed Front-End Engineering and Design for Alfanar‘s Lighthouse Green Fuels sustainable aviation fuel project in Teesside, UK.
Lighthouse Green Fuels – Project Background Lighthouse Green Fuels is planned as a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable naphtha refinery at Teesside.
CCS-Enabled Design and Teesside Infrastructure Interfaces The Lighthouse Green Fuels project is designed to be carbon capture and storage (CCS) enabled.
Global Low-Carbon Fuels Market Outlook – CF Intel Analysis Lighthouse Green Fuels sits within a low-carbon fuels market where front-end engineering is doing the hard work of separating investable projects from policy ambition.
Source: Worley Supporting Sources: Alfanar, Lighthouse Green Fuels
text:
Worley has completed Front-End Engineering and Design for Alfanar‘s Lighthouse Green Fuels sustainable aviation fuel project in Teesside, UK.

The completed FEED package moves the project into a more technically defined development phase ahead of a targeted Final Investment Decision by the end of 2027. Once operational, the facility is expected to produce around 180 million litres of sustainable aviation fuel and 30 million litres of renewable naphtha annually, with commercial operations expected in 2032.

Lighthouse Green Fuels – Project Background

Lighthouse Green Fuels is planned as a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable naphtha refinery at Teesside. Alfanar’s project materials describe the development as a brownfield refinery project that will convert sustainably sourced biomass, including forestry, sawmill and agricultural residues, into drop-in aviation fuel.

The project is being developed against the UK SAF mandate, which came into effect in January 2025 and targets SAF reaching 10% of UK jet fuel demand by 2030. Alfanar says this is equivalent to around 1.2 million tonnes of SAF per year, making domestic SAF production capacity a material industrial and fuels infrastructure issue for the UK market.

The planned facility is expected to process more than 1.5 million tonnes per year of sustainably sourced biomass feedstock. The process gasifies feedstock into synthesis gas, cleans the gas stream and uses Fischer-Tropsch synthesis to produce hydrocarbon waxes that are then upgraded into SAF and renewable naphtha.

FEED Scope and Project Definition

Worley’s FEED scope covered feedstock handling, gasification, Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, utilities, storage infrastructure and potential integration with Teesside’s emerging carbon capture and storage network. The engineering work was carried out by Worley’s UK team with support from its Global Integrated Delivery experts in India.

For project delivery teams, the significance of FEED completion is that it converts a process concept into a more defined technical and commercial basis. At this stage, scope, cost, schedule, execution strategy and interface risks become clearer before the project moves toward project financing, procurement and construction commitment.

Worley says the FEED phase is expected to reduce project risk and improve cost, schedule and execution certainty ahead of FID. In practical terms, the next major steps are the investment decision, contracting strategy, major equipment procurement, site execution planning and later notice to proceed milestones.

CCS-Enabled Design and Teesside Infrastructure Interfaces

The Lighthouse Green Fuels project is designed to be carbon capture and storage (CCS) enabled. Alfanar’s project page states that the core plant design removes carbon dioxide from the syngas stream so the Fischer-Tropsch reaction can operate efficiently, creating a high-purity carbon dioxide stream that is suitable for sequestration.

Alfanar also intends to capture carbon dioxide emissions from the on-site integrated power plant and send them to permanent storage. The interface with Teesside’s emerging CCS network is therefore more than an environmental feature; it is part of the industrial integration required for the plant’s low-carbon fuel pathway.

Worley’s scope did not stop at the process units. Feedstock handling, utilities and storage infrastructure are material delivery interfaces for a project of this type, particularly where biomass logistics, gasification, fuel upgrading, tankage, quay access and carbon capture systems need to work as one facility.

Global Low-Carbon Fuels Market Outlook – CF Intel Analysis

Lighthouse Green Fuels sits within a low-carbon fuels market where front-end engineering is doing the hard work of separating investable projects from policy ambition. Similar activity has been noted across early-stage fuels and hydrogen projects, including Technip’s FEED role on Jet Zero’s alcohol-to-jet SAF project in Australia, thyssenkrupp Uhde’s pre-FEED contracts for Fuella’s green ammonia projects in Brazil and Utility Global and SAMJIN E&I advancing the Daejeon H2Gen hydrogen project in South Korea.

The market signal is that alternative fuels projects are moving through increasingly detailed front-end gates before sponsors commit capital. For contractors and suppliers, the opportunity is not only in the future EPC contract packages; it is also in early engineering, process integration, feedstock logistics, storage systems, CCS interfaces and execution planning.

What to Watch

FID pathway: Alfanar is targeting FID by the end of 2027. The key test is whether the completed FEED package supports a financeable execution plan for a large, integrated biomass-to-liquids project.

CCS interface: Potential integration with Teesside’s carbon capture and storage network will be important for the project’s carbon intensity and industrial delivery model.

Supply chain readiness: Biomass feedstock logistics, gasification systems, Fischer-Tropsch units, utilities, storage and construction sequencing will all need to be aligned before major execution can proceed.

title: Why the Future of Sustainable Aviation Fuel Depends on Digital Feedstock Discovery
description:
For the better part of two decades, the biofuels industry has focused almost exclusively on one side of the equation.
Every refinery announcement, every Sustainable Aviation Fuel mandate, every airline commitment and every net-zero roadmap ultimately depends on one thing.
Every day, families cook meals, fry food and generate waste oil that is often discarded.
However, through the integration of digital collection infrastructure, they can also serve as community recycling centres.
By integrating collection infrastructure directly into operational workflows, these risks can be reduced substantially while simultaneously improving efficiency and traceability.
text:
For the better part of two decades, the biofuels industry has focused almost exclusively on one side of the equation.

We have debated technologies. We have debated refining pathways. We have debated regulations, mandates, carbon accounting methodologies, financing structures, certification systems and supply chains. Billions of dollars have been invested into developing technologies capable of converting waste and residue-based feedstocks into low-carbon fuels. Entire industries have emerged around refining, trading, certification and compliance.

Yet despite all this progress, one fundamental problem remains largely unsolved.

Where will the feedstock come from?

Every refinery announcement, every Sustainable Aviation Fuel mandate, every airline commitment and every net-zero roadmap ultimately depends on one thing. Feedstock.

Without feedstock, there is no renewable diesel.

Without feedstock, there is no Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

Without feedstock, there is no energy transition.

The reality is that the greatest challenge facing our industry today is not refining technology. The technology exists. The capital exists. The demand certainly exists. What does not yet exist at the scale required is a system capable of discovering, aggregating and mobilising enough sustainable feedstock to meet future demand.

For years, feedstock aggregation has been approached largely as a logistics exercise. Companies buy trucks, rent warehouses, hire drivers and attempt to build collection networks. While this approach may have worked when the industry was smaller, it is increasingly proving insufficient for the scale of the challenge that lies ahead.

The future of biofuels will not be won by those with the largest trucks. It will be won by those with the best data. The future belongs to those capable of discovering feedstock that nobody else can see. That is the lesson we have learned at FatHopes Energy over the last fifteen years.

When we first started collecting Used Cooking Oil, our world was relatively straightforward. The majority of available volumes were concentrated within the food and beverage sector. Restaurants, hotels, food courts, industrial kitchens and fast-food chains generated substantial quantities of waste cooking oil and represented the most logical starting point for any collection programme.

Like many others in the industry, we built our business around these commercial generators. We established collection routes, developed relationships with restaurant operators and invested heavily in logistics infrastructure. For many years, this model served us well.

However, as the biofuels industry matured, something began to change. Demand accelerated. What was once a niche industry became a strategic industry. What was once considered alternative became mainstream.

Governments introduced mandates. Airlines committed to decarbonisation targets. Investors began allocating capital. Refineries started appearing across multiple continents. Every new refinery required feedstock. Every new SAF producer required feedstock. Every new renewable diesel facility required feedstock.

Suddenly the same waste streams that had once been overlooked became highly sought after commodities. The challenge was no longer collecting feedstock. The challenge became finding more of it.

As we looked deeper into the problem, we realised something important. The future growth opportunity for our industry was not hidden within large industrial generators. It was hidden within millions of households.

Every day, households across Malaysia produce used cooking oil. Every day, families cook meals, fry food and generate waste oil that is often discarded. Historically, this oil has been poured down drains, thrown into rubbish bins or disposed of without a second thought.

Yet collectively, these small volumes represent one of the largest untapped feedstock resources available anywhere in the world. The problem is not that the resource does not exist. The problem is that it is fragmented.

Recovering twenty tonnes of used cooking oil from a fast-food chain is relatively simple. Recovering twenty tonnes from thousands of households is an entirely different challenge.

Traditional collection systems were never designed for this. The economics do not work. The logistics become overwhelming. The administrative burden becomes immense. The traceability requirements become almost impossible to manage. It was at this point that we realised something that would fundamentally change the direction of our company.

The future of feedstock aggregation would not be built on trucks. It would be built on technology. More specifically, it would be built on digital infrastructure.

For many years, digitalisation has transformed industries such as transportation, banking, retail and hospitality. Consumers now expect real-time visibility, instant transactions and seamless digital experiences in almost every aspect of their lives. Yet within the biofuels industry, many collection systems remained remarkably analogue.

Collection requests were managed through phone calls. Scheduling was coordinated through text messages. Collection records were maintained manually. Traceability often relied on paperwork. Performance data was fragmented across multiple systems. For an industry tasked with delivering one of the most important environmental solutions of our generation, the underlying infrastructure remained surprisingly outdated.

We believed there was a better way.

Almost ten years ago, we began building what has since evolved into a comprehensive digital ecosystem designed specifically for feedstock aggregation. Rather than developing a single application, we created a connected technology stack where every participant within the supply chain could interact through a common digital platform.

The objective was simple. Make feedstock discovery easier. Make feedstock collection more efficient. Make feedstock traceability absolute. Make participation accessible to everyone.

Today, that ecosystem consists of multiple applications serving different stakeholders throughout the value chain.

The Vendor App was developed for commercial generators such as restaurants, hotels, food courts and fast-food operators. Historically, these businesses relied heavily on manual communication whenever collections were required. Managers would call collectors, send messages or wait for routine collection schedules. There was limited visibility, limited accountability and little control over the process.

The Vendor App changed that entirely.

Collection requests can now be initiated instantly. Collection schedules can be managed digitally. Historical collection data is accessible at any time. Environmental impact metrics can be monitored continuously. Most importantly, collection vehicles can be tracked in real time, giving businesses visibility that previously did not exist.

The impact extends beyond convenience. By digitising interactions between generators and collectors, we have created a level of transparency that benefits every participant within the ecosystem.

Supporting this system is our Driver App, which acts as the operational backbone of our collection network. Every day, hundreds of collection vehicles navigate complex routes involving thousands of collection points across multiple regions. Historically, route planning depended heavily on human judgement and experience. While effective to a degree, this approach inevitably resulted in inefficiencies.

The Driver App allows routes to be optimised dynamically. Drivers receive collection assignments digitally. Volumes can be forecast. Vehicle utilisation can be monitored. Navigation support is integrated directly into operational workflows.

The result is lower operating costs, reduced emissions, improved service quality and higher recovery rates. Every unnecessary kilometre avoided improves both economics and sustainability. Every additional litre recovered strengthens the circular economy.

As important as commercial collections remain, the most exciting development within our ecosystem has undoubtedly been the emergence of household participation.

For decades, waste management has been viewed primarily as a disposal exercise. Society generated waste and then attempted to remove it as efficiently as possible. Very little attention was given to the latent value contained within these waste streams.

That mindset is now changing.

Through our Consumer App, households are able to participate directly in the circular economy. Individuals can locate collection points, schedule contributions, track their recycling activities and receive rewards for their participation. More importantly, they gain visibility into the environmental impact of their actions.

What was once considered waste now has value. What was once discarded now generates income. What was once an environmental liability has become a renewable resource. Perhaps the most profound outcome has been behavioural change.

We are witnessing an entire generation beginning to understand that sustainability and economic value are not mutually exclusive. Households are increasingly recognising that responsible environmental behaviour can also create tangible financial benefits.

This shift in mindset may ultimately prove more valuable than the feedstock itself. After all, sustainable industries are not built solely on infrastructure. They are built on participation. They are built on engagement. They are built on trust.

To further expand collection reach, we developed the Ranger App, enabling micro-aggregation at the community level. Rather than relying exclusively on centralised collection infrastructure, communities themselves become active participants in feedstock recovery. Local collection champions can aggregate material, coordinate participation and facilitate collection activities within their neighbourhoods.

This creates a distributed collection network capable of reaching feedstock sources that would otherwise remain inaccessible. In effect, every neighbourhood becomes a potential feedstock hub.

Every household becomes a potential contributor. Every citizen becomes a stakeholder within the energy transition. The implications of this model extend far beyond biofuels. They represent a blueprint for how circular economies can function at scale.

One particularly interesting outcome emerged through our collaboration with petrol station operators. Traditionally, petrol stations exist to distribute fuel. However, through the integration of digital collection infrastructure, they can also serve as community recycling centres.

When households deposit used cooking oil at participating locations, transactions are recorded digitally, rewards are distributed automatically and traceability is maintained throughout the process. What surprised us was the commercial impact.

Locations participating in these programmes experienced significant increases in customer engagement and footfall. Many contributors subsequently spent their rewards within the station’s convenience store, creating additional commercial value for retailers.

For perhaps the first time, sustainability, customer acquisition and commercial performance were aligned within a single ecosystem.

The same principle applies within the fast-food industry, where our collection technologies have significantly reduced the need for manual oil handling. Historically, transferring used cooking oil exposed staff to potential burn risks and operational hazards. By integrating collection infrastructure directly into operational workflows, these risks can be reduced substantially while simultaneously improving efficiency and traceability.

This is often overlooked when discussing innovation. Technology should not only improve margins. Technology should improve lives.

Perhaps the greatest benefit delivered by digital infrastructure is traceability. In an era where sustainability claims are increasingly scrutinised, the ability to verify feedstock origins has become essential. Every litre entering the biofuels supply chain must be accounted for. Every transaction must be transparent. Every participant must be accountable.

Our digital ecosystem enables precisely that. We know who contributed the material. We know where it originated. We know when it was collected. We know where it travelled. We know where it was delivered. This level of visibility creates trust across the entire value chain and strengthens the credibility of sustainable fuels as a whole. It also enables something equally important: accurate emissions measurement.

Because we understand the precise movement of material throughout the supply chain, emissions calculations can move beyond assumptions and approximations. Distances travelled, collection patterns and transportation activities can all be measured with significantly greater precision.

As regulators, investors and airlines demand increasingly sophisticated sustainability reporting, this capability will become indispensable.

Looking ahead, it is becoming increasingly clear that the future leaders of the biofuels industry will not necessarily be those with the largest refineries. They will be those with the strongest feedstock ecosystems. They will be those capable of discovering feedstock others cannot find, recovering feedstock others cannot access and tracing feedstock others cannot verify.

Feedstock discovery is rapidly becoming the most important competitive advantage within the industry. Technology is what makes that possible.

As Malaysia continues to position itself as a leader in sustainable aviation fuel and advanced biofuels, we have a unique opportunity before us. We can build not merely a refining industry, but an entire digital ecosystem capable of becoming the global benchmark for feedstock aggregation.

Imagine a future where every household participates. Every restaurant is digitally connected. Every collection is traceable. Every contributor is rewarded. Every litre recovered contributes towards decarbonising aviation.

That future is no longer theoretical. The foundations are already being built. The question is not whether digitalisation will transform feedstock aggregation. The question is who will lead that transformation.

At FatHopes Energy, we believe the answer begins with connecting every participant within the ecosystem and ensuring that nobody is too small to contribute. Because the future of Sustainable Aviation Fuel does not begin at the refinery.

It begins in the kitchen. It begins in the community. It begins with discovering value where others see waste. And if we get this right, Malaysia and Selangor will not simply participate in the global energy transition. They will become the benchmark by which the rest of the world measures itself.

title: Japan's JAL, ANA raise fuel surcharges to record levels | MarketScreener
description:

text:
Savannah-based business jet manufacturer Gulfstream has inaugurated its first dedicated customer support center at Seletar Airport in Singapore, in collaboration with Jet Aviation. This strategic move highlights Gulfstream’s confidence in the Asia-Pacific region, with Singapore positioned as a pivotal hub for the company’s expansion in business aviation.

Strategic Expansion in Asia-Pacific

Lor Izzard, Gulfstream’s Senior Vice President of Support, emphasized Singapore’s significance as a “natural choice given its role as a leading aerospace hub.” The newly established facility, situated within Jet Aviation’s Singapore premises, is staffed by a team of eight Gulfstream professionals, including customer technical managers, materials and quality specialists, a field service representative, and a regional sales manager. Izzard noted that having a dedicated on-site team enables Gulfstream to provide a more seamless and convenient service experience for customers throughout the region.

This support center complements Gulfstream’s existing 5,000-square-foot distribution facility in Singapore, which fulfills over 70% of regional parts orders and maintains an inventory exceeding $70 million in spare parts. This infrastructure not only supports repair operations but also advances Gulfstream’s long-term strategy to expand in-house component support capabilities.

Competitive Landscape and Market Dynamics

Gulfstream’s expansion occurs amid intensifying competition within the Asia-Pacific business aviation maintenance sector. Established competitors such as Bombardier are also enhancing their regional presence; notably, Bombardier recently announced a $100 million, 250,000-square-foot facility at Seletar Aerospace Park. Additionally, private aviation services provider WingsOverAsia has commenced construction on a maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) and innovation facility at Seletar, expected to be operational by 2027. This new facility will enable WingsOverAsia to service larger aircraft, including the Gulfstream G700 as well as Boeing and Airbus corporate jets.

Industry observers are closely monitoring how Gulfstream will leverage its Singapore facility to enhance service offerings and sustain its competitive advantage. The company faces the challenge of differentiating itself in a market where rivals are also investing heavily in customer support and infrastructure. Analysts anticipate that competitors may respond with increased marketing efforts and service improvements to safeguard their market share.

Recent Aircraft Debuts and Regional Commitment

The opening of the Singapore support center follows Gulfstream’s European debut of its next-generation G300 and G400 aircraft at Farnborough Airport, London’s business aviation hub, on June 9. Mark Burns, Gulfstream’s president, highlighted the jets’ “unmatched performance, efficiency and cabin innovation—capabilities that are ideally suited to operators in the region.”

Unveiled in September 2025, the super-midsize G300 features the longest cabin in its class, accommodating up to 10 passengers and offering a range of 3,600 nautical miles at Mach 0.80. The G400 set a city-pair speed record en route to Farnborough, flying 3,250 nautical miles from Washington, D.C., in just over six hours at an average speed of Mach 0.87, utilizing sustainable aviation fuel.

Through the establishment of its Singapore support center and the introduction of new aircraft models, Gulfstream is reaffirming its commitment to growth in the Asia-Pacific region, even as it navigates a dynamic and increasingly competitive market environment.

text:
Bio-energy is emerging as a key pillar of India’s green growth strategy and is set to play a crucial role in the country’s energy transition, Trade Promotion Council of India (TPCI) said on Sunday.

The council, on June 12, gathered policymakers, diplomats, industry leaders, energy experts, innovators, and stakeholders from across the bio-energy ecosystem to deliberate on strategies for accelerating India’s transition towards sustainable and energy-secure growth.

It said that the council has constituted a Bio-Energy Committee to bring together stakeholders across the sector, facilitate dialogue on policy and regulatory reforms, and recommend frameworks to accelerate adoption and unlock investment potential.

“Our goal is to strengthen India’s bio-energy ecosystem and align industry priorities with our national climate commitments, including the pledge to achieve net-zero emissions. Now is the time. Collaboration will be the key. Government, industry, and academia must work together to ensure innovation, affordability, and scalability,” TPCI Chairman Mohit Singla said.

He said that huge opportunities are there in the bio-energy sector, and it will help reduce dependence on fossil fuels while addressing waste management challenges.

From bio-CNG and ethanol blending to biomass power generation, this sector can significantly strengthen India’s clean energy mix, create rural employment and empower farmers, Singla said.

“Bio-energy is not merely an alternative fuel source; it is a strategic pillar of India’s green growth story, poised to become a cornerstone of our energy transition. Energy security, sustainability, climate resilience, and economic growth are no longer separate conversations. They are deeply interconnected,” he added.

Bio-energy is renewable energy derived from biological sources such as agricultural residues, crop waste, animal manure, forestry by-products, municipal organic waste and dedicated energy crops.

It can be converted into various forms of energy, including biofuels like ethanol and compressed biogas (CBG), electricity, heat and sustainable aviation fuel.

“Our goal is to strengthen India’s bio-energy ecosystem and align industry priorities with our national climate commitments, including the pledge to achieve net-zero emissions. Now is the time. Collaboration will be the key. Government, industry, and academia must work together to ensure innovation, affordability, and scalability,” TPCI Chairman Mohit Singla said.

He said that huge opportunities are there in the bio-energy sector, and it will help reduce dependence on fossil fuels while addressing waste management challenges.

From bio-CNG and ethanol blending to biomass power generation, this sector can significantly strengthen India’s clean energy mix, create rural employment and empower farmers, Singla said.

“Bio-energy is not merely an alternative fuel source; it is a strategic pillar of India’s green growth story, poised to become a cornerstone of our energy transition. Energy security, sustainability, climate resilience, and economic growth are no longer separate conversations. They are deeply interconnected,” he added.

Bio-energy is renewable energy derived from biological sources such as agricultural residues, crop waste, animal manure, forestry by-products, municipal organic waste and dedicated energy crops.

It can be converted into various forms of energy, including biofuels like ethanol and compressed biogas (CBG), electricity, heat and sustainable aviation fuel.

title: Thailand Sustainable Aviation Fuel Market Analysis
description:
Thailand’s sustainable aviation fuel industry is shifting from early projects to a rule-based market.
The Department of Energy Business is preparing to introduce new SAF standards and to make blending mandatory in jet fuel from 2026.
Under the framework, Jet A-1 fuel specifications and quality requirements at both production and sale stages will be split into three categories: conventional Jet A-1 fuel, fuel produced through co-hydroprocessing, and conventional Jet A-1 blended with pure SAF.
In this first phase, Thailand’s rules limit SAF production to HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids) technology.
For comparison, the European Union has enforced mandatory SAF blending for flights departing from EU airports, with a 2% blending requirement in place since 2025.
text:
Thailand’s sustainable aviation fuel industry is shifting from early projects to a rule-based market. The Department of Energy Business is preparing to introduce new SAF standards and to make blending mandatory in jet fuel from 2026. The regulations are set to come into force on January 1, 2026. Under the framework, Jet A-1 fuel specifications and quality requirements at both production and sale stages will be split into three categories: conventional Jet A-1 fuel, fuel produced through co-hydroprocessing, and conventional Jet A-1 blended with pure SAF. The department has also defined standards for SAF itself, aiming to ensure SAF produced and supplied in Thailand meets recognised international standards.

In this first phase, Thailand’s rules limit SAF production to HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids) technology. Feedstocks and production processes must comply with ASTM D7566 norms. Officials have framed this as a practical step, since Alcohol-to-Jet technology using ethanol is still under development and has not yet reached full commercial scale. The policy also aligns with ICAO efforts to encourage airlines worldwide to adopt SAF to reduce aviation emissions. Globally, aviation is responsible for approximately 2% of total carbon dioxide emissions and accounts for 12% of emissions from the transportation sector, underscoring why standards, traceability, and fuel quality are central to adoption.

Projects, Blending Timelines, and the Commercial Supply Base

Thailand already has projects that can anchor early supply as blending begins. Bangchak Corporation is building a HEFA SAF plant using used cooking oil as the primary feedstock. The project is designed for one million litres per day, or about 6,289 barrels per day, and is expected to be completed and begin commercial operations in the second quarter of 2026. PTT Global Chemical (GC) is producing SAF using co-processing HEFA technology, also based on used cooking oil, and the project is already operating commercially with an initial capacity of 16,438 litres per day, or about 103 barrels per day. These volumes matter because mandated blending creates predictable demand that can support ramp-up.

Thailand’s first SAF standard has been reported as expected to be released and enforced with blending that starts at 1% and increases to 8% by 2036. The move is positioned to decarbonize aviation in line with international measures and to support Thailand’s goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. For comparison, the European Union has enforced mandatory SAF blending for flights departing from EU airports, with a 2% blending requirement in place since 2025. These policy signals matter in a market that is still scaling globally, where SAF can be blended with conventional fuels at levels ranging from 10% to 50% depending on production method and feedstock.

Broader market indicators highlight why Thailand’s direction is attracting attention, even as local production ramps up in stages. Fortune Business Insights valued the global SAF market at USD 2.72 billion in 2025 and projected growth from USD 4.02 billion in 2026 to USD 40.09 billion by 2034, with a CAGR of 33.3%. In Asia-Pacific, BIS Research estimated the SAF market could reach $39.23 billion by 2033 from $0.38 billion in 2023, at a growth rate of 58.99% over 2023–2033. Regional supply potential is also being discussed: an ASEAN outlook cited SAF feedstocks such as used cooking oil, rice waste, cassava waste, and forestry residues, and noted HEFA is the most prevalent technology for producing SAF today, costing about twice as much as jet fuel, with feedstock the largest cost contributor.

title: How POET's Iowa Biorefineries Turn the State's Corn Into Fuel for the Country
description:
It was POET’s first plant in Iowa and, at the time, the largest dry-grind, farmer-owned ethanol plant in the state.
The acquired plants run bigger still: Arthur, Fairbank, Menlo, and Shell Rock each produce 131-132 million gallons a year, while Iowa Falls produces 112 million gallons.
Every year, that single facility produces 130 million gallons of bioethanol, 220,000 tons of distillers grains, five million gallons of distillers corn oil, and 75 tons of NexPro.
Iowa’s ethanol plants were the first stop for 62% of the state’s corn crop.
Reflecting years later on the ethanol plant in Coon Rapids, semiretired Howard Roe put it the way a banker might.
text:
In the late 1990s, Howard Roe kept watching trainloads of corn leave town. Roe, a banker in Manning, Iowa, and then-president of the Manning Betterment Foundation, knew the farmers around him were getting about $1.88 per bushel and shipping their crop out to be turned into something more valuable elsewhere. “So we started looking for alternatives that would allow us to add the value ourselves,” he recalled.

That search led Roe to Jeff Broin, the founder of POET, a South Dakota company that had been building ethanol plants since it started with a single facility in Scotland, South Dakota, in 1987. Roe, by his own account, “pestered him long enough that he finally decided to come down.” Broin went to Manning in 1998, and a farmer-led group went to work. By the spring of 2001, the group had attracted 440 investors and raised enough capital for a majority co-op ownership of a $55 million ethanol plant capable of producing 40 million gallons annually. They broke ground near Coon Rapids in June 2001, and the plant began grinding corn in August 2002. It was POET’s first plant in Iowa and, at the time, the largest dry-grind, farmer-owned ethanol plant in the state.

Photo Courtesy Midwest Partnership EDC

More than two decades later, that single farmer-owned plant has become a network. POET, now headquartered in Sioux Falls, operates 35 bioprocessing facilities in the Midwest. Iowa is home to the largest concentration of POET facilities; POET lists facilities in roughly a dozen Iowa towns, among them Coon Rapids, Hanlontown, Ashton, Emmetsburg, Jewell, Gowrie, and Corning. Some were built from the ground up. Others arrived later: in June 2021, POET acquired the bioethanol business of Flint Hills Resources, including six plants in Iowa and Nebraska – including in Arthur, Fairbank, Iowa Falls, Menlo, and Shell Rock – plus two terminals in Texas and Georgia, which lifted the company to 33 facilities and a 40 percent jump in capacity.

The output of that Iowa network is both large and local. The Corning, Gowrie, and Jewell plants each consume approximately 23-24 million bushels of locally grown corn to produce 90 million gallons of bioethanol annually. The acquired plants run bigger still: Arthur, Fairbank, Menlo, and Shell Rock each produce 131-132 million gallons a year, while Iowa Falls produces 112 million gallons.

POET estimates each of its bioprocessing facilities generates roughly $200 million in local economic impact annually, the kind of figure that shows up in a small county as corn bids, tax revenue, and payroll. Each also creates local jobs. Corning, Emmetsburg, and Hanlontown employ about 40 people each, representing an annual payroll of nearly $1.5 million in Hanlontown alone. The facilities also provide value-added markets for farmers, as POET alone purchases 7% of the annual U.S. corn crop from more than 30,000 farmers. It is also an investment in local communities. For example, the Coon Rapids facility represents a $55 million investment by the farmer-owners, with investors now numbering more than 450 producers and non-producers.

Photo Courtesy POET

Those plants make more than fuel. Corn arrives by the truckload, and what leaves is bioethanol for the nation’s fuel supply, along with a range of co-products: high-protein animal feed, corn oil, purified alcohol, and captured carbon dioxide. Ryan Cummings, the operations manager at POET’s Shell Rock plant, described the shift his crew made over the years in plain terms: “We took a plant making only bioethanol and transformed it almost into a feedmill.” That feed is not an afterthought. Shell Rock’s newest product, a corn fermented protein feed formerly called NexPro, ships worldwide, including, as general manager Kristin Clay noted, for use in aquaculture. Every year, that single facility produces 130 million gallons of bioethanol, 220,000 tons of distillers grains, five million gallons of distillers corn oil, and 75 tons of NexPro.

Stack those plants together with the rest of the state’s, and the scale becomes hard to overstate. Iowa is the nation’s leading ethanol producer, and the broader renewable fuels industry it anchors contributed more than $23.7 billion in output and $5.7 billion in value added in 2024, according to a study commissioned by the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association. The industry also supported more than 34,600 jobs, with average wages exceeding $76,000 per year, totaling $2.6 billion in labor income. Iowa’s ethanol plants were the first stop for 62% of the state’s corn crop. The state produced 4.6 billion gallons of ethanol in 2024, close to 30% of the national total.

For the farmers Howard Roe was thinking about, that is a market that stays in the neighborhood. And as POET frames it, “Creating a cleaner future means getting our hands dirty. It doesn’t mean that our work isn’t cutting-edge. It just means that our breakthroughs are covered in layers of dust, sweat, and good old-fashioned grit.” That same entrepreneurial spirit has helped make POET the world’s largest producer of biofuels, which the company calls “clean, renewable, American-made energy.” Bioethanol contains significantly fewer toxic compounds than many conventional fuel additives and reduces emissions by nearly 50% compared to gasoline. POET estimates that global bioethanol use reduces emissions by 110 million metric tons annually: “That’s like taking 20 million vehicles off the road each year.”

Photo Courtesy POET

The throughline across the decades is the one Roe started with, and it tends to get framed less as environmental policy than as independence. Bill Howell, who managed the Coon Rapids plant as of 2012, came to it after 12 years as an Air Force officer and another 12 with a major oil company. His read on the work was blunt. “We really need to be energy independent, which means renewable fuels, not just drilling a bunch more holes in the ground. That’s why I’m here. I’m really excited about the potential ethanol and renewable fuels give to our nation,” he told Vital, POET’s magazine. Broin used similar language at the grand opening of the Corning plant in May 2007, saying the milestone “makes our country a more secure place by reducing our need for foreign oil.” Sen. Chuck Grassley, who spoke at that ceremony, agreed, “Energy security is one of the nation’s top priorities, and I salute you for helping to lead the way.”

The industry’s next markets look outward. The Renewable Fuels Association and producers like POET are pushing for year-round sales of higher ethanol blends and for ethanol-to-jet sustainable aviation fuel, a pathway that LanzaJet proved at commercial scale in Georgia in 2024. Those markets could create additional demand for Iowa-grown corn.

Back in Manning, the idea was simpler than any of that. Keep the value home. Reflecting years later on the ethanol plant in Coon Rapids, semiretired Howard Roe put it the way a banker might. “It’s always been one of my goals to try to make things better than what they were. This is definitely one of those projects.”

title: Ethanol transition can shift to "Transport Energy Backbone" to shield India from oil shocks: KPMG
description:
The consultancy firm flagged an adaptive fuel system, multi-grade distribution and flex-fuel vehicles as critical to unlocking this role.
In such situations, ethanol can be redirected toward the transport fuel system to reduce exposure to higher import costs, acting as a substitute margin.'
India has built capacity, supply chains and distribution systems at scale through the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme.
That transition 'entails coordinated readiness across supply, demand, pricing, infrastructure, and vehicle technology,' KPMG said.
'The opportunity is to transition ethanol from a successful blending programme to an integrated component of the transport fuel system enhancing resilience, reducing exposure to external volatility, and strengthening long-term energy security.'
text:
New Delhi [India], June 14 (ANI): India's ethanol transition is entering its next phase, where the fuel can move from a blending component to a potential transport energy backbone capable of moderating exposure to external price shocks, KPMG said in a report titled 'Beyond E20. The consultancy firm flagged an adaptive fuel system, multi-grade distribution and flex-fuel vehicles as critical to unlocking this role.

'Under low price environments characterised by a supply glut, the system remains anchored at baseline blending levels, allowing the fuel mix to benefit from favourable import economics while enabling diversion of ethanol to alternative pathways such as Sustainable Aviation Fuel,' KPMG said.

'When global oil supply tightens due to production cuts by OPEC, crude prices tend to rise. In such situations, ethanol can be redirected toward the transport fuel system to reduce exposure to higher import costs, acting as a substitute margin.'

During acute disruptions like the Russia-Ukraine conflict and recent geopolitical tensions involving Iran, 'this flexibility becomes even more critical,' the report noted. 'Sudden constraints in global supply can lead to sharp price spikes, at which point the system's ability to scale ethanol utilisation through higher pool blends and flex-fuel pathways provides a mechanism to partially offset external volatility.'

KPMG said the foundation for this shift is already in place. India has built capacity, supply chains and distribution systems at scale through the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme. The next phase, however, requires two structural shifts. Expanding ethanol's role beyond blending, and moving from uniform E20 distribution to a multi-grade ecosystem for E85/E100. That transition 'entails coordinated readiness across supply, demand, pricing, infrastructure, and vehicle technology,' KPMG said.

Despite progress, the report flagged constraints holding back blends beyond E20: dependence on 1G food-linked feedstock that limits scalability; E20 acting as a demand ceiling with supply beginning to exceed absorption; pricing rigidity in a cost-based framework; infrastructure not designed for multi-grade fuels; and limited penetration of flex-fuel vehicles.

To move forward, KPMG said India must diversify feedstock beyond 1G, evolve pricing toward a hybrid model balancing market alignment with stabilisation, enable infrastructure for multiple fuel grades, and strengthen the vehicle ecosystem through flex-fuel deployment and regulatory alignment.

'India has already established one of the world's largest ethanol ecosystems. The challenge ahead lies not in incremental scale-up, but in system-level evolution,' the report concluded. 'The opportunity is to transition ethanol from a successful blending programme to an integrated component of the transport fuel system enhancing resilience, reducing exposure to external volatility, and strengthening long-term energy security.' (ANI)

text:
La compagnia aerea KLM Cityhopper ha effettuato, l’8 giugno 2026, il suo primo volo passeggeri utilizzando parzialmente il carburante e-SAF, ovvero l’electro-Sustainable Aviation Fuel. Cosa cambia con l’utilizzo di questo carburante e perché è una rivoluzione?

Con una nuova guerra in Iran, e il blocco dello Stretto di Hormuz, in tutta Europa è scoppiata una crisi dei carburanti - sia per i veicoli su gomma che per gli aeromobili. Le compagnie aeree hanno seriamente rischiato di rimanere a terra per tutta l’estate, l’industria ha così iniziato ad accelerare su soluzioni che non utilizzassero il normale petrolio greggio. Servono proprio a questo gli e-SAF: a rendere l’aviazione più sostenibile, la strada per il successo però è molto lunga...

In realtà, e-SAF è una sigla raccoglie al suo interno diversi carburanti sostenibili. Si tratta di un’alternativa “ecologica” rispetto al jetfuel standard, gli esperti però avvertono: “Non bisogna prendere questo evento con eccessivo ottimismo”. A oggi, infatti, c’è scarsa disponibilità di e-SAF, ci sono ritardi nella produzione su larga scala di questo carburante. Ma come si producono gli e-SAF? Parliamo di carburanti prodotti utilizzando energia elettrica green, dunque proveniente dal solare, dall’eolico e dall’idrico. Questa elettricità viene usata per estrarre idrogeno verde tramite elettrolisi; idrogeno che viene poi combinato con la CO2 catturata direttamente dall’aria per creare un greggio sintetico, che poi a sua volta viene raffinato in cherosene sintetico.

Sulla carta, si tratta di una vera e propria rivoluzione, è però presto per cantare vittoria. I prezzi degli e-SAF, infatti, sono attualmente fuori mercato: il prezzo è 8 volte superiore a quello del cherosene fossile tradizionale, 4 volte superiore ai SAF standard (la questione ricorda molto da vicino quella degli e-fuel per automobili). KLM Cityhopper per il suo primo volo e-SAF ha utilizzato appena 200 litri di carburante sintetico, una miscela al 5% rispetto al totale. E pensare che il primo volo passeggeri e-SAF era avvenuto nel 2021 con 500 litri, da Amsterdam a Madrid; nel mezzo, cinque anni di vuoto. Una goccia nel mare, insomma. Il carburante è stato prodotto dalla tedesca INERATEC, mentre MB Energy si è occupata della miscelazione. Il rifornimento è avvenuto presso l’aeroporto di Amsterdam-Schiphol, l’aereo infatti ha coperto la tratta Amsterdam-Amburgo. Vedremo se, prossimamente, l’utilizzo di questo carburante aumenterà oppure se i prezzi lo renderanno inutilizzabile.

text:
Bayer’s stock may be hugging its 200-day moving average, but the company itself is anything but stationary. Over the next few weeks, a trio of high-stakes events — a US Supreme Court ruling, a regulatory green light for a promising stroke drug, and an accelerated push into biofuels — could realign the narrative for the beleaguered German conglomerate. The shares ended the week at €36.06, just a whisker above the 200-day line of €35.99, yet roughly 5% below the 50-day average. On a year-to-date basis, the stock is down about 5%, reflecting the persistent uncertainty that has weighed on Bayer since the Roundup litigation began.

The most anticipated catalyst is the Supreme Court’s decision in the glyphosate case Durnell. Oral arguments were heard in late April, and a verdict is expected by the end of June. If the court rules in Bayer’s favour, the legal foundation for thousands of pending claims would collapse, effectively ending the multibillion-dollar cash drain that has plagued the company. Berenberg analysts assign a 60% probability of a favourable outcome and have raised their price target for the stock to €40.50, while maintaining a “Hold” rating. The financial impact is stark: in the first quarter alone, net cash outflows for settling PCB and glyphosate lawsuits reached €2.002 billion, up from just €66 million in the same period last year. That outflow drove group free cash flow to a negative €2.320 billion.

A separate, yet equally significant, development came on 11 June when the European Medicines Agency validated the marketing application for Asundexian, a novel oral anticoagulant designed to prevent strokes in high-risk patients. The filing is based on the Phase III OCEANIC-STROKE study, which showed a 26% reduction in stroke risk with no increase in major bleeding events. The strong safety profile could make Asundexian a compelling alternative to existing therapies. Approval would give Bayer a valuable new revenue driver in its pharmaceuticals segment, where the pipeline has been under intense scrutiny.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Bayer?

Meanwhile, the company is also reshaping its operations on multiple fronts. On 8 June, Bayer reshuffled the leadership of its Consumer Health division, appointing Analia de la Fuente as global chief data officer, David Tomasi as global chief commercial officer, Samantha Avivi as global chief marketing officer, and Trevor Thrun to lead the US business, the division’s largest market. The overhaul is part of an internal strategy dubbed “Road to Billions”, aimed at accelerating growth and shortening decision-making chains. Dr. Jost Reinhard will also move to lead the radiology unit within pharma starting 1 August.

In the biofuels arena, Bayer is accelerating its North American camelina programme — an oilseed used to produce renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel. The original target of reaching one million acres by the mid-2030s has been pulled forward, driven in part by a new partnership with energy giant BP. The company is also lining up contracts with mill operators to give farmers guaranteed offtake, a move designed to de-risk adoption.

Financially, the picture remains mixed. First-quarter group revenue rose to €13.405 billion, while EBITDA before special items climbed 9% to €4.453 billion. Consumer Health posted currency-adjusted sales growth of 5.3% to €1.491 billion, though EBITDA margin slipped slightly to 22.6% on higher marketing costs and currency headwinds. The US market remained soft. CEO Bill Anderson has reaffirmed the full-year outlook: revenue between €44.5 billion and €46.5 billion, and EBITDA before special items between €9.4 billion and €9.9 billion.

With the half-year report due in the coming weeks, investors will soon have a fresh set of numbers to digest. But the real inflection point remains the Supreme Court’s ruling. If it goes Bayer’s way, the shares could finally break free from the legal overhang that has constrained them for years. If it does not, the path forward becomes far murkier. Either way, the next few weeks should provide clarity — and volatility.

Through our partnership with Blue Ocean Club, we’re delivering precisely that: the freedom of the skies transitioning seamlessly into the serenity of the open sea. ”

— Dr. Christoph Lymbersky

ALBUQUERQUE, NM, UNITED STATES, June 14, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Limitless Sky, the independent private jet charter brokerage known for transparent pricing, rapid response, and seamless global travel, today announced the expansion of its groundbreaking Sea-to-Sky integrated luxury packages in partnership with Blue Ocean Club and Limitless Sea.

This collaboration redefines ultra-high-net-worth travel by offering end-to-end journeys that seamlessly blend private aviation with superyacht experiences. Clients can now book a single, cohesive itinerary: a private jet flight to premier coastal gateways such as Nice (for Monaco), Olbia in Sardinia, Palma de Mallorca, or St. Barths, followed by a direct helicopter transfer to a fully crewed luxury yacht waiting offshore. One dedicated advisor manages every detail—from wheels-up to sunset cocktails on the deck—eliminating the fragmentation common in traditional luxury travel planning.

"Our clients demand more than just a flight or a yacht charter—they want a continuous narrative of effortless luxury," said Dr. Christoph Lymbersky, Investor and Founder of Limitless Sky and CEO of 499X Capital. "Through our partnership with Blue Ocean Club, we’re delivering precisely that: the freedom of the skies transitioning seamlessly into the serenity of the open sea. Whether it’s a week cruising the Mediterranean or a tailored Caribbean escape, the experience feels curated, calm, and entirely personal."

Signature Itineraries and Exclusive Access

The Sea-to-Sky program features bespoke itineraries aligned with the world’s most prestigious events and destinations. Highlights include:

- Monaco Grand Prix Weekend: Private jet arrivals into Nice with pre-secured slots, helicopter transfers to superyachts positioned for optimal race viewing, and VIP hospitality packages coordinated through Blue Ocean Club networks.

- Mediterranean Summer Cruising: Jet from major hubs to Sardinia or Mallorca, then days aboard luxury yachts exploring hidden coves, with options for private chefs, wellness programs, and shore excursions.

- Caribbean Escapes: Winter routing to St. Barths or Antigua, combining transatlantic-capable aircraft with island-hopping by yacht for ultimate privacy and flexibility.

These packages leverage Limitless Sky’s access to a vetted global fleet—including long-range jets like the Gulfstream G650 and Bombardier Global series—alongside Blue Ocean Club’s curated superyacht inventory. Pricing is fully transparent with no hidden markups, and all operators meet the highest safety standards (ARGUS, Wyvern, or IS-BAO certified).

The program builds on Limitless Sky’s core strengths: thousands of charters arranged, 800+ repeat travelers, NBAA membership, and 24/7 dedicated advisory support. Clients benefit from the same speed and flexibility that define the brokerage, including integration with empty-leg opportunities for enhanced value on positioning flights.

Enhanced Companion Travel Options

To further personalize these Sea-to-Sky journeys, Limitless Sky offers a discreet travel companion service in partnership with Never Forget. This optional, confidential arrangement provides refined, multilingual companionship tailored to the client’s itinerary—whether for the private jet flight, yacht stay, or full multi-city experience—coordinated with complete discretion and the same professionalism as all other services.

Industry Context and Demand

The announcement comes at a time when high-net-worth travelers increasingly seek integrated, experiential luxury that minimizes logistical friction. Post-pandemic demand for private aviation and yacht charters has surged, with clients prioritizing privacy, sustainability options (including Sustainable Aviation Fuel where available), and seamless multi-modal journeys. Limitless Sky’s Sea-to-Sky model directly addresses this by reducing empty positioning legs where possible and optimizing routes for efficiency and environmental consideration.

Blue Ocean Club, renowned for its exclusive yachting experiences (as seen on blueoceanclub.com), brings unmatched expertise in Mediterranean and Caribbean superyacht operations, complementing Limitless Sky’s aviation prowess.

Availability and Booking

Sea-to-Sky packages are now available for immediate booking across the 2026 season and beyond. Interested clients can request a customized quote via the Limitless Sky website or by contacting the 24/7 charter desk. Early inquiries are recommended for peak event periods such as the Monaco Grand Prix, Cannes Film Festival, or high season in the Mediterranean.

Limitless Sky is an independent private jet charter brokerage offering on-demand flights, empty leg deals (up to 75% savings), and fully customized luxury travel worldwide. text:
cockpitkingofficial

Verified

1h

The aviation industry has just admitted something many experts have been warning about for years. ✈️

The airline sector’s goal of reaching net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 is now looking increasingly unlikely.

At a major industry summit this month, airline leaders warned that production of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) remains far below the levels needed to hit long-term climate targets. Airlines had expected SAF to become one of the biggest tools for reducing emissions, but supply is still only a tiny fraction of global aviation fuel demand.

Why does this matter?

Because aviation demand continues to grow.

Passenger numbers remain strong, airlines are ordering hundreds of new aircraft, and airports are expanding. But cleaner fuel production isn’t growing at the same pace.

The interesting part?

Modern aircraft like the Airbus A350 and Boeing 787 are already dramatically more fuel efficient than the aircraft they replace.

The challenge isn’t building more efficient planes.

It’s finding enough sustainable fuel to power them.

For years, the debate was whether aviation could reach net zero by 2050.

Now the debate is whether there is enough time left to make it happen.

Why It Matters

A Colombian airport operator has made its first move into Washington, registering to lobby on aviation issues through a firm with deep roots in international and defense affairs. Corporacion Aeroportuaria del Este SAS filed a new lobbying registration with Jones Group International LLC on May 1, 2026, and signed on Wednesday, June 10. The registration marks the company's debut in federal lobbying, entering at a moment when Congress is actively reshaping U.S. aviation policy in the wake of the deadliest domestic aviation disaster in decades.

By the Numbers

The lobbying registration lists no dollar amount for the filing period, consistent with a new client registration. One lobbyist is listed as active on the account, affiliated with Jones Group International LLC. No in-house lobbyists are disclosed. No prior lobbying spend by Corporacion Aeroportuaria del Este SAS appears in federal lobbying disclosure records, making this the company's first known federal lobbying compliance filing.

Broader Context

The backdrop for this lobbying registration is a Congress still responding to the January 29, 2025 midair collision between American Airlines Flight 5342 and a U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter near Reagan National Airport, which killed 67 people. That disaster triggered a sustained wave of aviation safety legislation throughout 2025 and into 2026.

Separately, House Transportation Committee Democrats raised alarms as recently as June 1, 2026, criticizing what they described as a plan by Secretary Mullin to divert international flights. That debate, involving international aviation routing policy, is directly relevant to the interests of a foreign airport operator.

The Agenda

The lobbying disclosure lists a single issue area: Aviation/Aircraft/Airlines. No specific issues or legislation are identified in the filing. Given the broad issue code and the absence of named bills, the precise scope of the company's federal lobbying agenda is not yet public. There are, however, active bills and congressional debates touching aviation safety, international flight routing, and FAA reform that are relevant to the issue area under which this registration falls

Between The Lines

Congressional aviation activity during the year before this registration was substantial. Key developments include:

The Rotorcraft Operations Transparency and Oversight Reform (ROTOR) Act, introduced by Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz in July 2025, passed the Senate unanimously in December 2025 but fell short of the two-thirds majority needed in the House in February 2026. The bill would require ADS-B safety technology and improve air traffic control oversight.

The Mental Health in Aviation Act passed the House in September 2025, requiring FAA reforms around mental health care for aviation professionals.

The Aviation Innovation and Global Competitiveness Act was introduced in February 2026 to streamline FAA certification for Advanced Air Mobility aircraft.

House Transportation Committee Democrats criticized a plan to divert international flights, with the Aviation Subcommittee's Democratic leaders speaking out in late May 2026.

Competitive Landscape

Major U.S. aviation stakeholders have been active throughout this legislative cycle. American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Boeing, the Air Line Pilots Association, Airlines for America, the Cargo Airline Association, and the National Air Traffic Controllers Association all submitted statements in support of the ROTOR Act during its Senate Commerce Committee markup. The Congressional Sustainable Aviation Caucus hosted a Member briefing in February 2026 featuring United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby on sustainable aviation fuel and emerging aviation technologies. No other foreign airport operators appear in the available lobbying disclosure records on the same issue area during this period.

The Bottom Line

Corporacion Aeroportuaria del Este SAS is a first-time entrant into federal lobbying, arriving during one of the more active periods for aviation policy on Capitol Hill in recent years. The registration is broad, covering aviation generally, with no specific bills or issues named. The choice of Jones Group International LLC, a firm oriented toward international and defense matters, signals the company's likely focus on U.S. engagement with international aviation policy. How the company's agenda takes shape will become clearer in subsequent lobbying disclosure filings.

text:
New Delhi: India's ethanol transition is entering its next phase, where the fuel can move from a blending component to a potential transport energy backbone capable of moderating exposure to external price shocks, KPMG said in a report titled "Beyond E20. The consultancy firm flagged an adaptive fuel system, multi-grade distribution and flex-fuel vehicles as critical to unlocking this role.

"Under low price environments characterised by a supply glut, the system remains anchored at baseline blending levels, allowing the fuel mix to benefit from favourable import economics while enabling diversion of ethanol to alternative pathways such as Sustainable Aviation Fuel," KPMG said.

Advt

"When global oil supply tightens due to production cuts by OPEC, crude prices tend to rise. In such situations, ethanol can be redirected toward the transport fuel system to reduce exposure to higher import costs, acting as a substitute margin."

During acute disruptions like the Russia-Ukraine conflict and recent geopolitical tensions involving Iran, "this flexibility becomes even more critical," the report noted. "Sudden constraints in global supply can lead to sharp price spikes, at which point the system's ability to scale ethanol utilisation through higher pool blends and flex-fuel pathways provides a mechanism to partially offset external volatility."

KPMG said the foundation for this shift is already in place. India has built capacity, supply chains and distribution systems at scale through the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme. The next phase, however, requires two structural shifts. Expanding ethanol's role beyond blending, and moving from uniform E20 distribution to a multi-grade ecosystem for E85/E100. That transition "entails coordinated readiness across supply, demand, pricing, infrastructure, and vehicle technology," KPMG said.

Despite progress, the report flagged constraints holding back blends beyond E20: dependence on 1G food-linked feedstock that limits scalability; E20 acting as a demand ceiling with supply beginning to exceed absorption; pricing rigidity in a cost-based framework; infrastructure not designed for multi-grade fuels; and limited penetration of flex-fuel vehicles.

Advt

To move forward, KPMG said India must diversify feedstock beyond 1G, evolve pricing toward a hybrid model balancing market alignment with stabilisation, enable infrastructure for multiple fuel grades, and strengthen the vehicle ecosystem through flex-fuel deployment and regulatory alignment.

"India has already established one of the world's largest ethanol ecosystems. The challenge ahead lies not in incremental scale-up, but in system-level evolution," the report concluded. "The opportunity is to transition ethanol from a successful blending programme to an integrated component of the transport fuel system enhancing resilience, reducing exposure to external volatility, and strengthening long-term energy security."

text:
Amerykańska firma Electra we współpracy z NASA stworzyła unikatowy koncept odrzutowego samolotu pasażerskiego. Hybrydowo-elektryczna konstrukcja ma latać o 17% efektywniej.

Branża lotnicza od lat szuka sposobów na ograniczenie zużycia paliwa i emisji CO₂ bez konieczności całkowitej rewolucji w istniejącej infrastrukturze lotniskowej. Teraz amerykańska firma Electra, specjalizująca się w napędach hybrydowo-elektrycznych, zaprezentowała koncepcyjny samolot pasażerski nowej generacji, który według analiz może zapewnić nawet 17% większą efektywność niż konstrukcje przewidywane na rok 2050 napędzany wyłącznie tradycyjnymi silnikami.

Projekt powstał w ramach programu NASA Advanced Aircraft Concepts for Environmental Sustainability (AACES) i stanowi próbę połączenia klasycznych silników odrzutowych z nowoczesnymi technologiami elektrycznymi.

Nietypowy kadłub, który sam generuje siłę nośną

Najbardziej charakterystycznym elementem nowej konstrukcji jest szeroki kadłub typu „double bubble” (podwójna bańka). W przeciwieństwie do tradycyjnych samolotów, gdzie za większość siły nośnej odpowiadają skrzydła, tutaj również sam kadłub aktywnie uczestniczy w utrzymywaniu maszyny w powietrzu.

Takie rozwiązanie pozwala zmniejszyć opór aerodynamiczny i poprawić ogólną wydajność lotu. Konstruktorzy twierdzą, że odpowiednie ukształtowanie kadłuba umożliwia wykorzystanie energii przepływającego powietrza znacznie efektywniej niż w obecnych samolotach pasażerskich.

Silniki odrzutowe współpracują z elektrycznymi wentylatorami

Projekt Electry wykorzystuje dwa silniki turbowentylatorowe umieszczone pod skrzydłami. Ich zadaniem nie jest jednak wyłącznie generowanie ciągu. Produkują one również energię elektryczną zasilającą wentylatory zamontowane w tylnej części samolotu.

Rozwiązanie wykorzystuje technikę określaną jako Boundary Layer Ingestion (BLI), czyli „pochłanianie warstwy przyściennej”. Wentylatory przechwytują wolniej poruszające się powietrze przepływające wzdłuż kadłuba i ponownie nadają mu energię, ograniczając straty aerodynamiczne.

Według analiz Electry takie połączenie klasycznego napędu odrzutowego z elektrycznym wspomaganiem może przynieść nawet 17-procentowy wzrost efektywności w porównaniu z przyszłymi konstrukcjami uwzględniającymi jedynie postęp w materiałach, aerodynamice czy technologii silników.

Samolot bez rewolucji na lotniskach

Jednym z głównych problemów wielu futurystycznych projektów lotniczych jest konieczność budowy zupełnie nowej infrastruktury. Electra chce tego uniknąć.

Nowa konstrukcja została zaprojektowana tak, aby mogła korzystać z istniejących bramek lotniskowych oraz obecnych procedur operacyjnych linii lotniczych. Samolot ma wykorzystywać standardowe paliwo lotnicze lub zrównoważone paliwa SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuel), bez potrzeby stosowania wodoru czy rozbudowanych systemów ładowania akumulatorów na lotniskach.

To podejście znacząco zwiększa szanse, że podobne konstrukcje mogłyby zostać rzeczywiście wdrożone do eksploatacji, zamiast pozostać jedynie efektownymi demonstratorami technologicznymi.

Większy komfort pasażerów

Interesującym aspektem projektu jest również układ kabiny. Dzięki nietypowemu kadłubowi konstruktorzy przewidują możliwość zastosowania dwóch przejść w samolocie należącym do klasy wąskokadłubowej.

Takie rozwiązanie mogłoby przyspieszyć boarding i opuszczanie pokładu przez pasażerów, a jednocześnie poprawić komfort podróży bez konieczności przechodzenia do znacznie większych i droższych samolotów szerokokadłubowych.

Otwarta technologia dla całej branży

Electra nie ograniczyła się wyłącznie do stworzenia koncepcji. Firma przygotowała również jedenaście opracowań technicznych opisujących zastosowane modele, metody i wyniki badań.

Przedsiębiorstwo wykorzystało także otwartoźródłowe narzędzie projektowe NASA Aviary, służące do wielodyscyplinarnej optymalizacji konstrukcji lotniczych. Dodatkowo opracowano zestaw narzędzi projektowych dla samolotów zelektryfikowanych, który ma zostać udostępniony szerszej społeczności badawczej.

Celem jest nie tylko rozwój pojedynczego projektu, ale przyspieszenie prac nad kolejną generacją ekologicznych samolotów pasażerskich.

Najwięksi gracze przemysłu wspierają projekt

W realizację programu AACES 2050 zaangażowano liczne instytucje przemysłowe i akademickie. Wśród partnerów znalazły się m.in. American Airlines, Honeywell Aerospace, Lockheed Martin, a także naukowcy z Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of Michigan oraz University of California, Irvine.

Tak szeroka współpraca pokazuje, że przemysł lotniczy coraz poważniej traktuje elektryfikację jako jeden z kluczowych kierunków rozwoju lotnictwa komercyjnego.

Trzecia era lotnictwa?

Według kierownictwa Electry świat stoi u progu „trzeciej ery lotnictwa”. Po epoce samolotów tłokowych i późniejszej dominacji napędu odrzutowego nadchodzi czas konstrukcji hybrydowych oraz elektrycznych.

Choć prezentowany projekt pozostaje na razie koncepcją, pokazuje kierunek, w którym mogą podążać samoloty pasażerskie w kolejnych dekadach. Jeśli założenia projektantów okażą się trafne, przyszłe maszyny będą nie tylko oszczędniejsze i bardziej ekologiczne, ale również wygodniejsze dla podróżnych — bez konieczności przebudowy światowej infrastruktury lotniczej.
