"Sudden constraints in global supply can lead to sharp price spikes, at which point the system's ability to scale ethanol utilisation through higher pool blends and flex-fuel pathways provides a mechanism to partially offset external volatility."

KPMG said the foundation for this shift is already in place. India has built capacity, supply chains and distribution systems at scale through the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme. The next phase, however, requires two structural shifts. Expanding ethanol's role beyond blending, and moving from uniform E20 distribution to a multi-grade ecosystem for E85/E100. That transition "entails coordinated readiness across supply, demand, pricing, infrastructure, and vehicle technology," KPMG said.

Despite progress, the report flagged constraints holding back blends beyond E20: dependence on 1G food-linked feedstock that limits scalability; E20 acting as a demand ceiling with supply beginning to exceed absorption; pricing rigidity in a cost-based framework; infrastructure not designed for multi-grade fuels; and limited penetration of flex-fuel vehicles.

To move forward, KPMG said India must diversify feedstock beyond 1G, evolve pricing toward a hybrid model balancing market alignment with stabilisation, enable infrastructure for multiple fuel grades, and strengthen the vehicle ecosystem through flex-fuel deployment and regulatory alignment.

"India has already established one of the world's largest ethanol ecosystems. The challenge ahead lies not in incremental scale-up, but in system-level evolution," the report concluded. "The opportunity is to transition ethanol from a successful blending programme to an integrated component of the transport fuel system enhancing resilience, reducing exposure to external volatility, and strengthening long-term energy security." text:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup, which kicked off this week (11 June), will span three countries, 16 cities and 104 matches.

It could become the most carbon-intensive World Cup in history, according to environmental analysts.

Scientists for Global Responsibility (SGR) believe the event could generate around nine million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in total emissions.

This is nearly double the historical average for tournaments between 2010 and 2022.

The carbon footprint is roughly equal to 6.5 million average British cars being driven for an entire year.

The expanded format includes 48 teams for the first time, up from 32 in 2022. This represents a 50% increase in the number of participating nations and adds 40 additional matches to the schedule.

The geographical spread of host cities stretches from Vancouver in the north to Mexico City in the south, and from the Pacific coast to the Atlantic seaboard.

This vast distance between venues creates unprecedented logistical challenges for teams, officials and supporters travelling between matches.

Air travel will account for a substantial portion of emissions due to the geographical spread across the US, Canada and Mexico.

Teams progressing deep into the tournament could travel thousands of miles between group stage matches and knockout rounds.

FIFA acknowledges that air travel is a significant contributor to the overall footprint of any major event, noting that "it is clear that reducing emissions linked to flights is one of the biggest sustainability challenges major event organisers face".

The organisation has explored alternatives including carbon offset programmes and sustainable aviation fuel initiatives.

However, the sheer scale of movement required across three countries makes meaningful reductions difficult to achieve within the current tournament structure.

Existing infrastructure reduces construction emissions

The North American hosts are using entirely existing stadiums rather than building new infrastructure.

This approach differs from tournaments in Qatar and Russia, which required purpose-built venues.

The decision eliminates carbon-intensive construction and avoids venues standing empty after the tournament ends. Several host stadiums have invested in renewable energy systems in recent years.

All 16 host venues are established facilities with existing transport links and hospitality infrastructure.

This includes iconic stadiums such as MetLife Stadium in New York/New Jersey, SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles and Azteca Stadium in Mexico City, which will become the first venue to host three separate World Cup tournaments

Making use of NFL stadiums

The reuse of existing infrastructure represents a significant departure from recent World Cup hosting strategies.

Qatar 2022 required the construction of seven new stadiums, whilst Russia 2018 saw the construction or substantial renovation of 12 venues for the tournament.

The Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, typically used for NFL games, will host eight matches including a semi-final.

The venue is the first professional sports venue in North America to earn LEED Platinum certification, the highest possible standard for sustainable building design.

More than 4,000 solar panels on campus generate around 1.6 million kilowatt-hours of renewable electricity a year.

The stadium has reduced overall electrical use by 29% through energy-efficient design.

A four-million-litre underground cistern captures rainwater for cooling and irrigation.

The system reduces demand on municipal water supplies whilst providing a sustainable source for maintaining the playing surface and surrounding landscape.

Arthur Blank, the Owner of the Atlanta Falcons, says of the venue: "We set out to build a venue that would not only exceed expectations but also push the limits of what was possible in terms of stadium design, fan experience and sustainability."

The stadium's retractable roof features a distinctive petal design that minimises the building's environmental impact when open.

Natural ventilation reduces the need for air conditioning during suitable weather conditions.

Houston pledges renewable electricity

In Texas, Houston's host committee has pledged to supply all main official tournament sites with 100% renewable electricity.

The commitment covers NRG Stadium and other venues in the city.

The pledge is notable given Houston's position as the energy capital of the US.

The city is home to the headquarters of many of the world's largest oil and gas companies.

NRG Stadium, home of the Houston Texans NFL team, will host six matches during the tournament, including fixtures from the round of 32 onwards.

The venue has a seating capacity of more than 72,000 for football fans.

Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, meanwhile, transitioned to 100% carbon-free electricity ahead of Super Bowl LVIII in 2024.

The venue sources renewable energy from the Copper Mountain Solar facility located approximately 40km south of the city.

Other host cities are following a similar approach for the World Cup.

However, the effectiveness of renewable energy credits as a climate solution remains debated among environmental scientists and campaigners.

Aramco partnership raises questions

FIFA's climate strategy, published in 2021, pledges to cut the organisation's emissions by 50% by 2030 and achieve net zero by 2040.

Environmental campaigners have questioned the commercial programme for this tournament.

Saudi Aramco is FIFA's exclusive energy partner under a four-year deal signed in 2024. The agreement is reportedly worth US$100m per year.

According to S&P Global, the Saudi state-owned oil giant accounts for 9-11% of global oil production.

The company produced 13.6 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2023.

Amin H. Nasser, its CEO, has argued that the world should continue investing in oil and gas rather than pursue accelerated phase-out timelines.

This position stands in direct opposition to recommendations from climate scientists regarding the pace of fossil fuel phase-out required to meet Paris Agreement targets.

The company has stated that its partnership with FIFA aligns with its goal of providing reliable energy to communities worldwide. Critics argue the partnership contradicts FIFA's green commitments.

The sponsorship deal has drawn criticism from climate activists, football supporters' groups and human rights organisations.

Several national football associations have faced pressure from environmental campaigners to speak out against the arrangement.

Steve Cockburn, Amnesty's Head of Economic and Social Justice, is critical of the firm's involvement.

However, the Aramco partnership and the scale of air travel emissions could undermine these efforts.

The question of how to balance spectacle with sustainability remains unresolved.

The tournament also faces scrutiny over fan travel patterns.

Supporters following their teams across multiple cities could generate substantial additional emissions beyond official tournament operations. FIFA's carbon accounting methodology has been questioned for potentially excluding certain categories of indirect emissions.

The energy implications will continue to play out beneath the surface throughout the tournament.

The opening match took place at Mexico City's Azteca Stadium, with the final scheduled for MetLife Stadium in New York/New Jersey on 19 July.

Between now and then, the world's attention will focus on the football, whilst the environmental legacy of this expanded format will only become clear in the years that follow.

text:
The brothers took over leadership of Henderson Land Development and utility Hong Kong and China Gas, known as Towngas, from their father Lee Shau Kee, who died in March 2025 at the age of 97. Forbes estimated the brothers' combined fortune at $34.9 billion in February, placing them second on the Hong Kong rich list, a position previously held by their father.

Since becoming co-chairmen in 2019, they have guided the family business through major challenges, including the Covid-19 pandemic, an economic slowdown and changes in the property market while pursuing investments in clean energy and sustainability.

Although both oversee Henderson Land and Towngas, Peter has emerged as the driving force behind the group's push into renewable energy, sustainable fuels and climate technology. "While real estate continues to provide stable returns, future growth momentum will increasingly come from emerging sectors such as green tech," Peter said in a February interview with Forbes.

He said green technology could support both the environment and the family's businesses by leveraging Towngas' expertise as Hong Kong's dominant piped-gas supplier and an operator of city-gas networks in mainland China.

Under his leadership, Towngas has accelerated investments in renewable energy and low-carbon technologies. The company operates more than 1,000 solar projects across Hong Kong and mainland China, with total grid-connected solar capacity reaching 2.6 gigawatts as of June 2025. Sales of solar-generated electricity rose 44% year-on-year in the first half of 2025.

The utility has also expanded into green fuels, converting waste tires, biomass and municipal waste into green methanol for shipping while producing hydrogen from synthetic and landfill gas for transportation and EV charging infrastructure. Green methanol production capacity reached 165,000 tons last year and is expected to double by 2028.

In April this year, the company launched Hong Kong's first hydrogen-powered EV charging system for a commercial building at its headquarters in North Point, according to The Standard. The system uses locally produced hydrogen to generate electricity for EV chargers, allowing older buildings to add charging facilities without extensive upgrades to their power infrastructure.

Among the group's most prominent clean-energy ventures is EcoCeres, a Hong Kong-based producer of sustainable aviation fuel made from used cooking oil and animal fats. The company says its fuel can reduce greenhouse-gas emissions by up to 90% compared with conventional jet fuel and currently supplies about 20% of the global sustainable aviation fuel market.

Beyond Towngas, Peter has invested in climate technology through Full Vision Capital, a family office he founded in 2014. The firm had backed 10 green-technology startups with a combined valuation of $6.5 billion as of December 2025, according to Towngas chief investment officer Alan Chan.

Its investments include California-based EnerVenue, which develops long-duration energy storage systems for renewable energy. Towngas plans to deploy the company's batteries at EV charging stations in Hong Kong and mainland China.

The family office has also invested in Hong Kong-based i2Cool, whose solar-reflective coatings and energy-saving window films are being used at Towngas facilities and Henderson Land properties to lower electricity consumption. Another investment, Shanghai-based StarFive Technology, develops energy-efficient semiconductor chips used in Towngas smart gas meters.

The sustainability strategy extends beyond energy. In May, Henderson Land secured Hong Kong's first biodiversity loan for its Central Yards development, according to the South China Morning Post. The financing, estimated at around HK$100 million ($12.8 million), will support the planting of about 400 trees and 280 plant species, along with biodiversity monitoring and urban forest management programs.

Located on Hong Kong's Central waterfront, the project will include more than 300,000 square feet of open green space, including the district's largest elevated garden. The first phase is expected to open in 2027.

Betting on long-term growth

Despite the expansion, green technology remains a relatively small contributor to Towngas' earnings. Traditional gas operations still account for more than three-quarters of the utility's revenue.

In the first half of 2025, Towngas reported revenue of HK$27.5 billion and net profit of HK$3 billion. While its renewable energy business remained profitable, green fuel operations recorded an operating loss of HK$190 million.

Analysts nevertheless expect the sector to gain momentum as governments and businesses intensify efforts to reduce carbon emissions. HSBC analyst Evan Li said Towngas' green businesses are likely to expand faster than its conventional gas operations over time, supported by economies of scale and policy support.

The brothers remain confident that the strategy will deliver long-term growth.

"Five years from now, with our commercial developments in Central completed and green energy projects gradually taking shape, I'm confident our prospects will look bright," Martin said.

Peter, the father of three teenage boys and a devout Buddhist, added: "In the long run, we are going for the industries the Earth needs most."

Savannah-based business jet manufacturer, Gulfstream, has partnered with Jet Aviation to open its first dedicated customer support centre at Seletar Airport in Singapore.

The establishment of Gulfstream’s on-site customer support facility in Singapore reflects the OEM’s confidence in Asia-Pacific, and Singapore specifically, as a long-term strategic growth market.

Singapore a “natural choice” for Gulfstream

Noting that the business is seeing increased activity across Asia, Lor Izzard, senior vice president, Gulfstream Support, described Singapore as a “natural choice given its role as a leading aerospace hub.”

The OEM has teamed up with Jet Aviation – one of its six authorised service centres – to open its dedicated customer support centre at the latter’s Singapore site. The office is staffed by a team of eight Gulfstream professionals, including customer technical managers, materials and quality team members, a field service representative and a regional sales manager.

Having a dedicated on-site team allows Gulfstream to deliver a more seamless and convenient service experience for customers across the region,” said Izzard.

The new support centre will complement Gulfstream’s existing 5,000 sq ft distribution centre in Singapore. This facility is responsible for fulfilling more than 70% of regional parts orders, housing more than US$70 million in dedicated spare parts inventory, supporting repairs and advancing Gulfstream’s long-term strategy to expand in-house component support.

The opening of Gulfstream’s new Singapore facility follows the announcement on 9 June by Bombardier that it is opening a US$100m, 250,000 sq ft facility at Seletar Aerospace Park.

Earlier this year, private aviation services provider WingsOverAsia also broke ground on an MRO/ Innovation facility at Seletar. Expected to be operational by 2027, it will enable WingsOverAsia to handle larger aircraft such as the Gulfstream G700 as well as Boeing and Airbus corporate jets.

Gulfstream debuts G300 and G400 at Farnborough

The announcement of its Singapore facility follows Gulfstream marking the European debut of its G300 and G400 next-generation aircraft at Farnborough Airport – London’s dedicated business aviation hub – on 9 June.

Mark Burns, president of Gulfstream, said the two jets “deliver unmatched performance, efficiency and cabin innovation – capabilities that are ideally suited to operators in the region.”

Unveiled in September 2025, the super-midsize G300 boasts the longest cabin in its class and seats up to 10 passengers. It combines class-leading range and speed – 3,600nm at Mach 0.80 or 3,000nm at Mach 0.84 – with short-field agility, opening up new routes and expanding access to challenging airports.

Meanwhile, the G400 flies farther and faster than any other aircraft in its class. En route to Farnborough from Washington, D.C., the G400 set its first city-pair speed record, completing the 3,250nm flight in just six hours and 12 minutes at an average speed of Mach 0.87, using sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

Gulfstream celebrates a trio of announcements with 100th G700 delivery

It’s been a busy week for the business jet OEM. Gulfstream also delivered its 100th G700.

“As deliveries have increased, so has customer demand,” said Burns. The 100th delivery, he added, set a new benchmark, “firmly establishing the G700 as the business aviation industry flagship.”

The delivery of the aircraft also marked the 100th G700 city-pair speed record, connecting Savannah with San Jose, California, in four hours and 36 minutes at an average cruise speed of Mach 0.91. The aircraft then flew from San Jose to Teterboro in New Jersey in a record four hours and 14 minutes at the same Mach speed.

description:

This breakthrough marks a world-first for aviation and positions Rolls-Royce at the forefront of zero-carbon flight technology.
Rolls-Royce and easyJet confirmed a successful simulated flight from start-up to landing using nothing but hydrogen fuel.
The engine held its full-rated take-off thrust of 15,250 lb on 100% hydrogen across the complete flight cycle.

text:
Rolls-Royce (LSE: RR.) shares could be on track for further gains after the company’s latest revelation rocked the aviation world. The aerospace giant has achieved what was once considered impossible: running a modern jet engine at full take-off power on pure hydrogen alone.

This breakthrough marks a world-first for aviation and positions Rolls-Royce at the forefront of zero-carbon flight technology.

Could this be the boost it needs to reverse months of stagnant price growth?

What exactly happened at the test?

Rolls-Royce and easyJet confirmed a successful simulated flight from start-up to landing using nothing but hydrogen fuel. They used a modified Pearl 15 engine at NASA’s Stennis Space Center in Mississippi.

Other tests have tried this before but never succeeded at full power. The engine held its full-rated take-off thrust of 15,250 lb on 100% hydrogen across the complete flight cycle.

This programme has given us the clearest understanding in the industry of how hydrogen behaves in a modern aero gas turbine

Adam Newman, Chief Engineer of Rolls-Royce’s Hydrogen Demonstrator Programme.

A green energy game-changer

This development is another nail in the coffin for oil and similar fossil fuels. Burn hydrogen cleanly and what emerges is water vapor – not less CO₂, but none of it.

Combustion keeps the turbomachinery the industry has spent a century refining while changing only the fuel chemistry. This maintains the power-to-weight ratio that makes gas turbines worth flying.

For FTSE 100 investors, this translates to tangible benefits:

Rolls is already posting exceptional results, and looks likely to continue:

Underlying operating profit reached £3.5bn up 40% from 2024.

Revenue came in at £20.1bn, up 14% year-on-year.

Free cash flow reached £3.3bn.

Analysts haven’t glossed over the development, with UBS in April eyeing a price target of 1,400p and Bank of America still holding a target of 1,600p set in February.

But how commercially viable is hydrogen-powered aviation?

The challenges ahead

A hydrogen-powered airliner is still a long way off. Proving an engine can run on hydrogen on a test stand isn’t the same as revenue service.

Hydrogen is one strand of easyJet’s decarbonisation plan leaning far more heavily on newer Airbus A320neo jets, sustainable aviation fuel, and operational efficiency.

text:
100% Ethanol Fuel Vehicles: The government has taken another step towards introducing vehicles that run entirely on ethanol, as regulations for 100 per cent ethanol fuel have now received legal approval. Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari shared this information, stating that the move would help reduce dependence on imports.

Speaking at a press conference in Nagpur, Minister Gadkari said he had signed the file to provide a legal framework for 100 per cent ethanol fuel vehicles. The move is part of the government's broader push to promote alternative fuel options.

"Last night at 8 PM, I signed the file making rules for 100% ethanol and giving it legal process," Gadkari said.

Push to Reduce Fuel Import Dependence

The minister said India currently spends around Rs 22 lakh crore on fuel imports and stressed the need to develop domestic alternatives.

"The country has an import of 22 lakh crores. Now, the resolution we made to reduce this import... gradually gas will also be produced in the country. An alternative to petrol and diesel will also be ready," he said.

Also Read: Big Update for Vehicle Owners: Government eases rules for car modifications and imports

Automakers Preparing 100% Ethanol Vehicles

Highlighting progress in the sector, Gadkari said a flex-fuel version of the Maruti Suzuki WagonR capable of running on 100 per cent ethanol has already been showcased.

"I am pleased to share that I had the opportunity to launch the Maruti Suzuki WagonR running on 100% ethanol," he said.

The minister added that several automobile manufacturers are preparing vehicles that can operate entirely on ethanol. According to him, companies including Toyota, Suzuki and Hyundai are expected to introduce such vehicles in the coming months.

"In the next two months, companies such as Toyota, Suzuki, and Hyundai will also launch vehicles that run entirely on 100% ethanol," Gadkari added.

In the two-wheeler segment, he noted that three out of five ethanol-powered motorcycles introduced so far belong to Hero MotoCorp, with two Hero models already launched on 100 per cent ethanol.

"Among the motorcycles launched, three out of five are from Hero MotoCorp, and two of Hero's motorcycles have already been launched on 100% ethanol," he further said.

Gadkari Recalls Early Scepticism Around Ethanol

Speaking about his long-standing support for ethanol-based fuels, Gadkari said the idea initially faced criticism and scepticism.

"I used to talk about this dream, and people used to laugh. Some friends even used to criticize it. I'll tell you a good story about how efforts are made to defame ethanol," he said.

The minister also referred to what he described as misinformation regarding ethanol fuel. Recalling an incident, he said a vehicle owner was told by a mechanic that ethanol was responsible for a diesel jeep breaking down.

"One person called me and said his jeep had broken down. When he took it to the mechanic, the mechanic said the car broke down because of putting ethanol in it. I asked him if his car runs on petrol or diesel. He said diesel. I said, 'We don't even put ethanol in diesel, so how did it break down?' So, many attempts were made to spread misinformation," Gadkari said.

Focus on Alternative Fuels

The government's efforts are aimed at expanding the use of alternative fuels and reducing reliance on conventional fossil fuels. Gadkari expressed confidence that ethanol would emerge as a viable alternative to petrol in the coming years.

Beyond road transport, he has also spoken about the potential of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), produced from biomass, as a future fuel option for the aviation sector.

title: España convertirá el humo de las fábricas en 'gasolina' para aviones - La Razón

Al frente de esta misión en España se encuentra Silvia Morales de la Rosa, investigadora del Grupo de Energía y Química Sostenible.
Su gran valor diferencial es que busca demostrar, en condiciones reales, cómo convertir emisiones de CO2 en combustibles sostenibles para barcos y aviones».
«Los primeros análisis del ciclo de vida del proceso STEROPE indican reducciones del 90-95% en emisiones, siempre que se utilice hidrógeno verde producido con energías renovables».
No se trata solo de tecnología, sino de convertir un problema –el CO2– en una gran solución energética.
text:
Imagine que las chimeneas de una refinería no fueran el final de un proceso contaminante, sino el principio de un viaje. Imagine que el dióxido de carbono (CO2), ese gas que calienta el planeta, pudiera ser atrapado en el aire y «cocinado» de nuevo hasta convertirse en el líquido transparente que mueve las hélices de un barco o las turbinas de un avión. No es ciencia ficción, es la realidad que se gesta en los laboratorios del Instituto de Catálisis y Petroleoquímica (ICP) del CSIC. Al frente de esta misión en España se encuentra Silvia Morales de la Rosa, investigadora del Grupo de Energía y Química Sostenible. Con la claridad de quien confía en que se puede cambiar el mundo, la doctora en CIencias Químicas explica que el proyecto europeo STEROPE es el puente que necesitábamos. «Esto no es solo un experimento en laboratorio. Su gran valor diferencial es que busca demostrar, en condiciones reales, cómo convertir emisiones de CO2 en combustibles sostenibles para barcos y aviones».

Habrá tres plantas piloto para demostrar que la tecnología es escalable a nivel Europa. La primera ya se encuentra instalada en el ICP español, y hay otras dos en construcción: una en la Universidad de Génova (Italia) –encargada de cazar el CO2– y otra en la de Gante (Bélgica), que transformará el metanol en combustible para la aviación. El proceso, según detalla la experta, se basa en tecnologías avanzadas y el uso de hidrógeno verde. La parte clave de este proceso es la que sucede, precisamente, en nuestro país.

Y es que, en el campus del CSIC en Madrid, el equipo de la Dra. Morales ha logrado un hito de ingeniería: una planta piloto que cabe en un contenedor estándar. «Hemos construido una unidad transportable, diseñada para operar en un contenedor estándar y que puede ser transportado a diferentes instalaciones». Esta «fábrica en una caja» es la encargada de producir el metanol, y pronto viajará a la refinería de Eleusis, en Grecia, para unirse a las otras piezas del rompecabezas en Italia y Bélgica.

A grandes rasgos, Morales explica el proceso completo: «En primer lugar, se captura y purifica el CO2. Posteriormente, el CO2 reacciona con hidrógeno en condiciones de presión y temperatura elevadas mediante un proceso catalítico, generando metanol y agua». Ese metanol ‘made in Spain’ es el «ingrediente base». Puede alimentar barcos directamente o, tras pasar por otro complejo proceso químico, transformarse en SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuel), el combustible que los aviones necesitan para despegar sin dejar una huella de carbono fósil.

«Básicamente, primero convertimos el metanol en olefinas... que luego se someten a otros procesos catalíticos (hidrogenación e hidroisomerización) y son estos combustibles sintéticos los que luego se probarán en turbinas de aviones». Es, en esencia, reciclar el aire para volver a volar.

Este esfuerzo conjunto entre países de la zona euro tiene un objetivo claro: la independencia. «La crisis energética ha puesto sobre la mesa una prioridad: ganar independencia frente al petróleo y al gas importados, en Europa y en España. En este contexto, los combustibles sintéticos aparecen como una solución estratégica».

Sin petróleo fósil en 2050

La normativa de la Unión Europea es una cuenta atrás: para el año 2050, el 70% del combustible de aviación debe ser renovable. STEROPE no solo busca cumplir la ley, sino superarla. Los análisis iniciales son asombrosos: mientras la norma exige reducir un 70% las emisiones, este proyecto apunta más alto. «Los primeros análisis del ciclo de vida del proceso STEROPE indican reducciones del 90-95% en emisiones, siempre que se utilice hidrógeno verde producido con energías renovables».

Para los escépticos que creen que esto solo alarga la vida de las refinerías, Morales es tajante: mientras no existan aviones eléctricos comerciales, esta es la solución más real que tenemos. «Sectores como la aviación o el transporte marítimo no tienen hoy alternativas eléctricas viables. Por lo que... esta sería una de las soluciones más inmediatas que tenemos ya muy cerca del mercado». Y España tiene una ventaja competitiva clave que nos posiciona en el mercado.

Gracias a nuestro sol y viento, podemos producir la cantidad de hidrógeno verde que necesita este proceso. El proyecto STEROPE, con sus 7 millones de euros de presupuesto, es el campo de entrenamiento para que España lidere esta carrera. «Si las pruebas funcionan, el salto a plantas semicomerciales podría darse en pocos años», asegura la investigadora.

Lo que el equipo del CSIC está construyendo es una forma de cerrar el círculo. No se trata solo de tecnología, sino de convertir un problema –el CO2– en una gran solución energética. La próxima vez que vea la estela de un avión en el cielo, piense que, gracias a científicas como Silvia, esa estela podría haberse producido «reciclando humo».

text:
Bio-energy is emerging as a key pillar of India's green growth strategy and is set to play a crucial role in the country's energy transition, Trade Promotion Council of India (TPCI) said on Sunday.

The council, on June 12, gathered policymakers, diplomats, industry leaders, energy experts, innovators, and stakeholders from across the bio-energy ecosystem to deliberate on strategies for accelerating India's transition towards sustainable and energy-secure growth.

It said that the council has constituted a Bio-Energy Committee to bring together stakeholders across the sector, facilitate dialogue on policy and regulatory reforms, and recommend frameworks to accelerate adoption and unlock investment potential.

"Our goal is to strengthen India's bio-energy ecosystem and align industry priorities with our national climate commitments, including the pledge to achieve net-zero emissions. Now is the time. Collaboration will be the key. Government, industry, and academia must work together to ensure innovation, affordability, and scalability," TPCI Chairman Mohit Singla said.

He said that huge opportunities are there in the bio-energy sector, and it will help reduce dependence on fossil fuels while addressing waste management challenges.

From bio-CNG and ethanol blending to biomass power generation, this sector can significantly strengthen India's clean energy mix, create rural employment and empower farmers, Singla said.

"Bio-energy is not merely an alternative fuel source; it is a strategic pillar of India's green growth story, poised to become a cornerstone of our energy transition. Energy security, sustainability, climate resilience, and economic growth are no longer separate conversations. They are deeply interconnected," he added.

Europe loves rules. That is often said with a sigh, especially in technology circles. While the United States builds fast and China scales hard, Europe regulates. AI Act, Cyber Resilience Act, Digital Markets Act, GDPR, NIS2: the list can feel endless. At the EU Digital Summit in Brussels, IO+ editor Mauro Mereu heard the central question repeated in many forms: is Europe regulating itself out of the digital race, or is it quietly building the conditions for long-term leadership?

The answer is not simple. Companies rightly warn that fragmented and overlapping regulation slows them down. Compliance can become a burden, especially when a single incident triggers multiple legal frameworks at once. But the Brussels discussions also showed another side. Trust, security, transparency and sovereignty are not soft values in the AI era; they are becoming infrastructure. People and companies will only use technologies they can rely on. In that sense, Europe’s regulatory instinct may turn from handicap into strategic advantage.

That will only happen if Europe learns to regulate with purpose. Rules must not merely prevent harm; they must also enable the kind of technology Europe wants to build: AI for drug discovery, climate data, industrial strength, public trust and verifiable human needs. GDPR once seemed like a burden but has become a global benchmark. The AI Act could do the same, but only if enforcement is consistent, simplification is taken seriously, and regulation serves innovation rather than standing beside it.

title: Wildlife Tourism Boom Reshapes Eco-Aviation Amid Flight Chaos
description:
Wildlife Tourism Becomes a 401 Billion Dollar Powerhouse Wildlife and nature-based travel is evolving from a niche interest into one of tourism’s most powerful segments.
Eco-Aviation Claims Rise Alongside Private Jet Emissions The expansion of wildlife tourism and private flying has unfolded alongside intensifying debate over aviation’s climate footprint.
Conservation Finance Gains, but Inequality Deepens For conservationists and destination communities, the wildlife tourism boom offers both crucial funding and complex trade-offs.
Observers say this dynamic raises questions about who ultimately benefits from the 401 billion dollar wildlife tourism boom.
Wildlife tourism is surging toward the 401 billion dollar mark, promising vital conservation income and unique nature experiences.
text:
A projected surge in wildlife tourism spending to around 401 billion dollars over the next decade is colliding with worsening airport disruption and a rapid rebound in private jet use, creating an emerging travel divide in which affluent flyers are increasingly shielded from the chaos facing commercial passengers.

Wildlife Tourism Becomes a 401 Billion Dollar Powerhouse

Wildlife and nature-based travel is evolving from a niche interest into one of tourism’s most powerful segments. Recent market analysis indicates the dedicated wildlife tourism sector could exceed 400 billion dollars in annual value by the mid-2030s, with some forecasts pointing to approximately 401.9 billion dollars worldwide as rising incomes, social media visibility and post-pandemic demand for open-air nature experiences converge.

Broader assessments of nature-based tourism suggest an even larger economic footprint. International conservation groups and economic studies describe nature-focused trips as generating hundreds of billions of dollars a year in direct and indirect spending, including park fees, guides, ecolodges, transport and local services around protected areas. This spending, in turn, underpins millions of jobs in communities that host safaris, marine wildlife expeditions and rainforest lodges.

Publicly available briefings from conservation organizations stress that this revenue is increasingly cited as a justification to protect habitats and wildlife, from African savannahs to coral reefs and mountain reserves. Governments and park agencies are framing wildlife tourism as a way to connect conservation finance with development goals, particularly in lower-income regions where visitor dollars can diversify rural economies.

Analysts note that a significant share of this new growth is concentrated in long-haul, higher-spend segments. Affluent travelers booking multi-country safaris, private wildlife cruises or bespoke conservation itineraries drive disproportionately high per-trip spending, which ties the expansion of wildlife tourism closely to premium and private aviation services.

Airport Chaos Pushes High-End Travelers Toward Private Skies

At the same time that wildlife tourism spending has accelerated, disruption across commercial aviation has remained pronounced. Industry and passenger-rights reports reviewing recent peak travel seasons highlight summers in which roughly four in ten passengers worldwide experienced some form of delay or cancellation, with even higher disruption levels in the United States and Europe during certain months.

Weather volatility, air traffic control constraints, staffing challenges and high-profile IT outages have combined to create recurrent “meltdown” scenarios at major hubs. In one notable episode, a global software failure in 2024 triggered cascading cancellations and delays across carriers and airports, leaving large numbers of passengers stranded and reviving questions about aviation resilience.

These recurring shocks have reinforced a pattern in which the most time-sensitive and high-spend travelers increasingly turn to private aviation to avoid congested terminals and volatile schedules. Data compiled in sustainability-focused research and industry trackers show private jet activity not only recovered faster than commercial traffic after the pandemic but has continued to grow, with some sources recording double-digit percentage increases in global private flights compared with pre-2020 baselines.

For elite wildlife tourists, the result is a bifurcated system. While mass-market travelers planning once-in-a-lifetime trips to safari destinations or island reserves must navigate complex connections and potential disruptions, the wealthiest visitors are booking point-to-point private flights directly into regional airports or bush strips that sidestep the most congested hubs altogether.

Eco-Aviation Claims Rise Alongside Private Jet Emissions

The expansion of wildlife tourism and private flying has unfolded alongside intensifying debate over aviation’s climate footprint. Peer-reviewed research on private aviation emissions shows that business and leisure jets account for a growing share of overall aviation climate impact, despite serving a small fraction of travelers. Studies of recent years in the United States and Europe, for example, indicate that private flights represent several percent of combined commercial and private aviation emissions, with emissions growth outpacing that of scheduled airlines.

Industry groups and manufacturers have responded with an ambitious eco-aviation narrative. Public communications emphasize the promise of sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, more efficient aircraft and carbon offsetting tied to conservation projects. Test flights using high blends or full replacement of fossil jet fuel with certified SAF have demonstrated substantial reductions in particulate emissions and contrail-forming ice crystals, suggesting potential climate benefits if such fuels were scaled up.

However, independent analyses note that SAF still represents a tiny fraction of global jet fuel use, and that much of the current marketing around private jets and sustainability outpaces actual uptake. Reports from policy institutes and environmental organizations describe a risk that “green” messaging around eco-aviation obscures the sector’s rising absolute emissions, particularly in premium segments such as luxury safaris and conservation-themed private tours.

This tension is especially visible in wildlife tourism, where airlines, tour operators and destination marketing bodies increasingly promote “low-impact” or “regenerative” itineraries even as the long-haul flights required to reach remote ecosystems remain the most carbon-intensive component of the trip.

Conservation Finance Gains, but Inequality Deepens

For conservationists and destination communities, the wildlife tourism boom offers both crucial funding and complex trade-offs. Recent policy papers on sustainable tourism describe nature-based travel as a major source of finance for protected areas, with revenues often reinvested into anti-poaching patrols, habitat restoration and local infrastructure. In regions where public conservation budgets are limited, high-value visitors are helping to keep parks open and rangers employed.

Yet the reliance on high-spend, fly-in clientele creates structural inequalities. Local residents, seasonal workers and budget travelers remain exposed to the full brunt of airline disruptions and price volatility. When major carriers cancel routes or reduce capacity, the shock can cut off access to markets and essential services for remote communities, even as private jets continue to arrive at nearby airstrips with minimal interruption.

Environmental advocates also warn that the concentration of wealthier visitors in fragile ecosystems amplifies pressures on wildlife if growth is not carefully managed. International monitoring of World Heritage and other flagship sites has flagged tourism, alongside invasive species and climate change, as a leading threat to some of the planet’s most important natural areas. Managing visitor numbers, aircraft noise, and the expansion of high-end lodges and airstrips becomes more challenging as demand increases.

Observers say this dynamic raises questions about who ultimately benefits from the 401 billion dollar wildlife tourism boom. While elite flyers may enjoy seamless eco-branded journeys insulated from crowded terminals and congested hub airports, many of the people and places that make these trips possible remain on the front line of both climate risk and transport instability.

Pressure Mounts for Stricter Climate and Travel Standards

Regulators are starting to respond to the collision of booming eco-tourism, aviation disruption and climate concerns. In the United States, the Federal Aviation Administration has finalized rules that will require new large jets and turboprops certified from the late 2020s to meet stricter fuel-efficiency and carbon standards, aligning with a national aviation climate action plan that targets net-zero sector emissions by 2050. Similar measures in Europe mandate a rising blend of sustainable aviation fuel in jet fuel supplied at major airports.

Despite these moves, climate researchers argue that technology and fuel switching alone are unlikely to keep aviation emissions in line with global warming limits if demand continues to rise, particularly in premium segments. Calls are growing for progressive levies on frequent flying and private jets, tighter regulation of eco-claims in aviation marketing, and greater transparency about the real climate impact of “once-in-a-lifetime” wildlife journeys.

For now, the trends are moving in parallel rather than in sync. Wildlife tourism is surging toward the 401 billion dollar mark, promising vital conservation income and unique nature experiences. Airport disruption continues to test the patience of mainstream travelers, incentivizing the growth of a largely unregulated private jet market. Eco-aviation technologies are making incremental progress but from a very low baseline.

How policymakers, industry and travelers reconcile these forces over the coming decade will determine whether the global eco-aviation boom genuinely supports conservation and fair access to nature, or primarily serves as a shield that allows a privileged minority to bypass the turbulence of an overburdened air travel system.

text:
Responsible: ad hoc news Companies & Analysis Desk. Reviewed prior to publication on June 13, 2026 at 6:38:33 PM ET. Details in the imprint.

Neste Oyj is in focus at the end of the week after securing a 250 million euro long-term loan from the Nordic Investment Bank (NIB) to support research and development in renewable solutions and to expand liquid plastics waste processing at its Porvoo refinery in Finland. The financing package, which runs for 10 years, is structured as a 150 million euro committed tranche plus an additional 100 million euro facility that Neste can draw as projects progress. Against this backdrop, Neste shares were among the weakest names in Helsinki on Friday, sliding around 4.7 percent to close near 27.7 euros, even as the broader OMX Helsinki 25 index ended higher.

NIB financing underscores Neste's capex priorities in renewable fuels and plastics recycling

The new NIB loan adds another building block to Neste's long-term funding structure as the company pushes deeper into renewable fuels, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and advanced plastic recycling technologies. According to coverage of the deal, the 10-year facility is designed specifically to fund R&D initiatives and capital investments that enable Neste to process larger volumes of liquid plastic waste at its Porvoo refinery, a core industrial hub for the group. Strategically, the move aligns with Neste's stated ambition to grow its renewable and circular solutions portfolio while gradually reducing exposure to traditional oil products.

NIB is positioning the loan as support for projects that have both environmental and innovation angles, including work on advanced feedstocks and process technologies that can cut lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. For Neste, earmarking a dedicated funding line for these efforts can help smooth capital expenditure planning and reduce refinancing risk in a period of heavy investment. The company has been investing in expanded renewable capacity at sites in Europe and North America in recent years, and R&D linked directly to commercial plants is a recurring theme in its investor presentations.

Structurally, the financing is divided into a firm 150 million euro tranche available upfront and a 100 million euro component that Neste can call upon subject to project milestones and capital needs. This kind of staged structure gives management flexibility to ramp spending in line with actual progress in plastics recycling and related R&D rather than locking in the full amount from day one. It also allows NIB to monitor the deployment of funds against environmental and technological objectives as the program advances.

Reports on the agreement emphasize that the plastics recycling element focuses on turning liquid plastic waste into usable refinery feedstock, effectively closing part of the loop in the plastics value chain. For an integrated player like Neste, being able to convert waste streams into inputs for higher-value fuels or chemical products can improve margins over time while supporting regulatory and customer demand for lower-carbon offerings. Market observers note that the loan therefore touches both the sustainability profile and the long-term earnings potential of the group, even if short-term share price reactions remain dominated by broader sector dynamics.

The loan comes at a time when European refiners and energy companies face increasing capital needs to adapt to climate policy, emissions rules, and evolving customer requirements. Access to long-dated funding from institutions like NIB can lower average financing costs for projects that might not attract the same terms in conventional bank or bond markets. For Neste, locking in 10-year money provides visibility over a significant slice of its innovation and circular-economy capex budget, complementing existing liquidity and credit lines disclosed in its financial reports.

According to prior investor communications, Neste has set clear strategic targets around renewable products and circular solutions, including scaling up production capacity for renewable diesel and SAF, as well as integrating more waste and residue feedstocks. The Porvoo refinery is central to this roadmap, not just as a processing asset but also as a testbed for new technologies that can later be replicated across the network. In that context, the NIB financing acts as a targeted tool to accelerate specific initiatives rather than a broad balance sheet backstop.

Market coverage of the deal indicates that, while the financing is strategically supportive, the immediate stock price reaction has been relatively muted compared with the size of the balance sheet. The loan amount, while material, represents a fraction of Neste's total assets and market capitalization, so investors appear to be treating it as an incremental positive rather than a thesis-changing event. Some commentary highlights that the agreement reinforces confidence in Neste's ability to tap specialized lenders for green and transition projects, which may matter more over the medium term than the headline figure alone.

From a capital structure perspective, adding a 10-year loan modestly increases gross debt but also extends the average maturity profile, which can be beneficial in a higher interest rate environment. Detailed terms such as pricing and covenants have not been widely disclosed in public summaries, but NIB's mandate generally involves supporting projects that promote competitiveness, sustainability, and innovation in the Nordic region, typically at market-based but stable conditions. For equity holders, the key question is whether the funded projects can generate returns above the cost of capital; the R&D and plastics recycling focus suggests that payback may be back-end loaded and contingent on successful commercialization.

Analysts following the stock will likely incorporate the loan into their models as part of Neste's broader capital spending envelope rather than as a standalone catalyst. Because the NIB facility is earmarked for specific projects, it may influence assumptions about future depreciation, R&D capitalization, and potential incremental earnings from new product lines. Coverage earlier this year already pointed to elevated investment levels in renewable platforms as a driver of near-term free cash flow pressure but also as a lever for longer-term growth. The new financing does not change that narrative but adds clarity on how part of the spending will be funded.

For investors watching the stock, the NIB loan highlights how much of the Neste story is now tied to the execution of its transition strategy rather than short-term refining margins. Share price performance can still be sensitive to diesel cracks, feedstock costs, and macro indicators, but incremental news flow is increasingly centered on sustainability-linked projects, regulatory developments, and innovation partnerships. In this context, dedicated funding for plastics recycling and R&D is a piece of a larger puzzle that markets will monitor over several years rather than quarters.

On the trading side, Friday's market data show that Neste was among the worst performers in the STOXX Europe 600 and on the OMX Helsinki 25, even though the Finnish index itself ended the session higher. According to one summary of the Helsinki close, Neste fell by about 4.67 percent, or roughly 1.36 euros, to trade around 27.74 euros at the end of the day. A separate indication from the Tradegate platform, where Neste is traded in euros as an off-exchange venue, shows last trades around 27.85 euros on June 12, 2026, suggesting comparable levels across different trading venues. These levels place the stock noticeably below previous recent highs and reflect both company-specific news flow and broader sentiment toward European energy and chemicals names.

While the one-day move is significant, it also needs to be seen in the context of Neste's wider trading history and volatility. Historically, the stock has experienced periods of sharp gains and pullbacks as markets recalibrated expectations for renewable fuel margins, policy support, and competitive dynamics. Technical-oriented services that track Neste's Finnish listing have highlighted relatively high day-to-day fluctuations, with daily swings of several percentage points not uncommon. Against that backdrop, a roughly 4 to 5 percent drop tied to a mix of sector pressure and company updates is notable but not unprecedented.

Benchmark data show that, on the day Neste declined, the STOXX Europe 600 index itself saw mixed performance across sectors, with some energy and industrial names also under pressure. Within the STOXX Europe 600, Neste appeared on lists of the steepest decliners, alongside other energy and industrial stocks. This underlines that stock-specific news like the NIB financing is interacting with broader risk-off or sector-rotation forces rather than acting in isolation. For portfolio managers, the move may represent either a reason to reassess exposure to European transition-focused energy plays or a temporary dislocation within a longer investment thesis.

Index-wise, Neste is part of major Nordic and European benchmarks, including the OMX Helsinki 25, which tracks the largest and most traded stocks on the Helsinki exchange. On the session in question, the index rose about 1.53 percent, indicating that local Finnish equities overall were in positive territory even as Neste lagged. Being a constituent of such indices means that flows from exchange-traded funds and passive vehicles can amplify moves when sector or country allocations shift. Additionally, as global investors adjust weightings among traditional oil, integrated energy, and renewables-oriented companies, names like Neste can see correlated moves that go beyond company-specific headlines.

In terms of valuation, the latest price levels imply a lower market capitalization than during earlier peaks in the renewable fuels cycle, when enthusiasm for green transition plays drove multiples higher. Without reproducing detailed multiples, market data and prior research hint that the stock has de-rated compared with those highs, reflecting more cautious assumptions about margin sustainability and capital intensity. The interplay between elevated capex, such as that supported by the NIB loan, and returns on invested capital is central to how valuation models are being recalibrated.

It is worth noting that, while the NIB financing focuses on R&D and plastics recycling, the company still operates a sizeable conventional refining business that is exposed to cyclical factors. Refining margins can be volatile, driven by global demand, crude spreads, and regulatory changes, and they still influence near-term earnings and cash flow. As a result, investors looking at news about long-term funding and innovation projects will typically weigh it alongside updated views on near-term margin trends, inventory effects, and hedging positions reported in quarterly results.

From a risk perspective, channeling substantial capital into new technologies and recycling solutions carries execution and market risks. Projects can face delays, cost overruns, or technological hurdles, and regulatory frameworks that support circular-economy investments can evolve over time. Nevertheless, lenders like NIB usually require a clear project pipeline and robust environmental and economic justifications before committing funds, which in turn provides some external validation of the strategic direction. For equity investors, the loan is neither a guarantee of success nor a red flag on its own, but rather a signal that stakeholders beyond shareholders see merit in Neste's project portfolio.

Looking ahead, the next major checkpoints for assessing the impact of the loan will be future quarterly updates and investor presentations where management provides more detail on the progress of plastics recycling projects at Porvoo and related R&D milestones. Metrics that may draw attention include the volume of waste and residue feedstocks processed, the share of renewable and circular products in total output, and any disclosed returns or margins on new product lines. Over time, evidence that these NIB-backed initiatives are generating stable cash flows could support a re-rating, while setbacks could feed into more cautious assumptions about capital efficiency.

For now, the key takeaway is that Neste has secured long-term, purpose-linked financing to support its transition agenda at a time when markets are scrutinizing both the pace and profitability of such transformations. Investors following the stock will likely track how efficiently the company converts this funding into commercial progress in renewable fuels and plastics recycling, while also keeping an eye on broader market conditions and energy-sector sentiment.

Overall, the combination of a targeted 10-year NIB loan and a notable one-day share price drop underlines the dual nature of the Neste investment case: structurally tied to long-term decarbonization and circular-economy themes, yet tactically exposed to cyclical and sentiment-driven swings. How these forces balance out over the coming quarters will be shaped not only by macro factors but also by the pace at which the Porvoo projects and other funded initiatives move from R&D into scaled, profitable operations.

Und die gibt es derzeit nicht.« Elisabeth Engelbrechtsmüller-Strauß Echter Binnenmarkt fehlt Es fehle zudem die Etablierung eines echten Binnenmarkts, der weder beim Flugverkehr, bei der Bahn, bei der Energie noch bei einem gemeinsamen Finanzmarkt existiere.
text:
Europa steckt in einer tiefen Krise, ausgelöst durch Überregulierung und eine Gesetzesflut von der EU. Wie Strategien zurück zu einem wettbewerbsfähigen Europa aussehen können, besprach Rainer Nowak, Geschäftsführer „Die Presse“, mit Elisabeth Engelbrechtsmüller-Strauß, CEO, CFO und Eigentümerin von Fronius, Günther Ofner, Vorstandsdirektor der Flughafen Wien AG, und Severin Gruber, Generalsekretär im Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft, Energie und Tourismus.

Österreich, Deutschland und die Schweiz sind die Länder mit der höchsten Pro-Kopf-Rate an Hidden Champions, also eher unbekannten mittelständischen Unternehmen, die in ihrer jeweiligen Nische Europa- oder Weltmarktführer sind. Ein solcher Hidden Champion ist Fronius mit Sitz im oberösterreichischen Pettenbach. Mithilfe seiner Pro­dukte lässt sich Sonnenenergie in Wechselstrom umwandeln.

Hidden Champions zeichneten sich durch ihre Kreativität und Innovationskraft aus, ist Elisabeth Engelbrechtsmüller-Strauß überzeugt. Hinzu komme der Mut, neue Ideen zu verfolgen und umzusetzen: „Fronius ist ein Technologieunternehmen und immer nur durch Innovation gewachsen. Ein wesentlicher Bestandteil ist die Strategie: Sie muss konstant bleiben und stetig verfolgt werden, auch wenn sie an veränderte Rahmenbedingungen angepasst wird.“

Auf dem Weg zur DDR 2.0

Günther Ofner ist überzeugt, dass unternehmerische Initiative viele Probleme bei den Rahmenbedingungen ausgleichen könne, aber nicht alle. Europa stecke in dem Dilemma, dass es jahrzehntelang von günstigen Energiequellen profitiert habe und davon ausgegangen sei, dass der Rest der Welt jene Maßstäbe befolgt, die Europa setzt. „Diese Voraussetzungen gibt es nicht mehr. Hinzu kommt, dass mit dem Austritt Großbritanniens jener Teil der Europäischen Union weggefallen ist, der den Regulierungsirrsinn zuvor blockiert hat. Seit dem Austritt wurden 6.000 Gesetzgebungsakte auf europäischer Ebene gesetzt, von denen ein großer Teil ideologiegetriebener, von links-grünen NGOs diktierter Schwachsinn ist“, kritisiert Ofner. „Der Zugang der Kommission und großer Teile des Parlaments zu wirtschaftlicher Tätigkeit ist ein Generalverdacht gegen Unternehmen und Konzerne, und der Versuch, alles mit über­bordenden Regeln fest­zunageln. Gehen wir diesen Weg weiter, sind wir in Europa auf dem Weg zu einer DDR 2.0.“

Auch wenn bereits die ersten Omnibus-Richtlinien, die Unternehmen massiv von Bürokratie entlasten sollen, in Kraft seien, ortet Ofner darin nur marginale Verbesserungen. „Beim Green Deal hat sich nicht wirklich etwas verändert. Wir machen weiter wie zu Beginn der 2020er-Jahre, obwohl sich alle Voraussetzungen seit damals grundlegend geändert haben.“ Die Annahme, alle anderen Nationen würden Europa folgen, wenn es vorangehe, hätten sich in Luft aufgelöst: „Niemand folgt uns, absolut niemand.“ Ofner ist bei der Flughafen AG für den Einkauf – und damit für Hunderte Millionen Euro – verantwortlich: „Bei dem Ankauf von neuen Bussen sind chinesische Anbieter zwischen 30 und 40 Prozent billiger als jene aus der EU. So patriotisch kann ich als ­börsennotiertes Unternehmen gar nicht sein, um das zu ignorieren.“

Das Problem der Flut an EU-Richtlinien und Verordnungen ist Severin Gruber aus eigener Erfahrung bekannt. „Wir leiden selbst zum Teil unter den vielen Richtlinien und Verordnungen, die wir umsetzen müssen. Es gab Zeiten, in denen ich in jeder Woche eine neue Behörde hätte gründen können. Damit sind wir selbst überfordert.“ Es gebe sehr viele, ambitionierte Ziele, die aber mit anderen euro­päischen Zielen nur schwer vereinbar und wohl nicht erreichbar seien. „Die Gefahr besteht, dass, wenn man sich überambitionierte Ziele setzt, die Politik damit aufhört, mit der Umsetzung zu beginnen“, sagte Gruber. Oft werde vermutet, dass Abgeordnete daran gemessen würden, wie viele Gesetze sie beschließen. „Man kann aber auch Gesetze beschließen, mit denen andere Gesetze abgeschafft werden. Das ist das gleiche Verfahren und zumindest genau so kompliziert. Vielleicht ist das das Problem“, führte der Generalsekretär aus. „Für den Omnibus, bei dem etwas abgeschafft werden soll, sind die gleichen langen Verfahren, die gleichen langen Diskussionen und die gleichen Abstimmungen auf Regierungsebene nötig. Das macht das System träge.“

Engelbrechtsmüller-Strauß moniert, dass in China eine Industriepolitik betrieben werde, mit der Unternehmen unterstützt würden, um erfolgreicher zu sein. Ähnlich sei es in den USA. „In Europa gibt es die Idee, wie man Unternehmen niederreglementieren kann. In den vergangenen Jahren bekamen wir eine Verordnung nach der anderen und es sieht nach der Intention aus, dass wir uns selbst abschaffen“, mahnte die Fronius-Eigentümerin. Es wäre viel wichtiger, in innovative Mitarbeiter zu investieren.

Günther Ofner ortet ein ideologisches Problem: „Europa ließ sich in den 2010er-Jahren von NGOs und ähnlichen Gruppen in eine Richtung treiben, die Unternehmer als halbkriminell ansehen und die den Freiraum und die Freiheit möglichst minimieren und einschränken wollen. Hinzu kam die Finanzkrise im Jahr 2008. Die USA haben sie mit marktwirtschaftlichen Mitteln gelöst, Europa hat sich dazu entschieden, alles zu regulieren und jedes Risiko auszuschalten. Unser Problem ist, dass wir den Menschen misstrauen, Freiheit schief ansehen und unternehmerische Tätigkeit unter einem ideologischen Generalverdacht steht.“

»Für einen Aufbruch braucht es eine positive Stimmung. Und die gibt es derzeit nicht.«

Elisabeth Engelbrechtsmüller-Strauß

Echter Binnenmarkt fehlt

Es fehle zudem die Etablierung eines echten Binnenmarkts, der weder beim Flugverkehr, bei der Bahn, bei der Energie noch bei einem gemeinsamen Finanzmarkt existiere. Ofner: „Experten haben errechnet, dass die faktischen Handelsbarrieren innerhalb der EU einem Binnenzoll von 41 Prozent entsprechen.“

Severin Gruber unterstrich, dass das Wirtschaftsministerium daran interessiert sei, Barrieren im EU-Binnenmarkt abzubauen, doch gewichtige Player in den Mitgliedstaaten mit manchen Handelshemmnissen gut leben könnten: „Spricht man über einen gemeinsamen Finanzmarkt, sind manche Institute darüber nicht sehr glücklich. Spricht man über Berufszugangsbeschränkungen oder den Zugang zum Markt, dann sind etablierte Unternehmen zuweilen skeptisch, diese abzubauen.“

Positive Stimmung nötig

Zur unglücklichen Gemengelage komme hinzu, dass Unternehmen, die in die EU exportieren, nicht ihren Regularien unterlägen. Engelbrechtsmüller-Strauß: „Ein unfairer Kampf. Für einen Aufbruch braucht es eine positive Stimmung. Und die gibt es derzeit nicht.“

text:

More than half of the professionals responsible for airline operations, safety, and fleet decisions in the United States admit they have only a general understanding of ADS-B In technology, despite widespread confidence that their airlines are prepared for a future mandate.

According to a new Acron Aviation report, nearly half of US airlines have already equipped at least part of their fleets with ADS-B In, while another 40% are actively evaluating the technology. Yet the study found that 51% of airline leaders describe their knowledge of ADS-B In as limited or only at a top level.

The findings raise questions about airline readiness for an ASD-B In mandate. The ALERT Act, which passed the US House of Representatives and is awaiting Senate approval, would require most commercial aircraft to be equipped with ADS-B In by December 31, 2031.

What is ADS-B In?

Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) is a surveillance system that uses satellite-based positioning to provide highly accurate aircraft location information.

Commercial aircraft operating in US-controlled airspace have been required to carry ADS-B Out equipment since January 2020. ADS-B Out continuously broadcasts an aircraft’s position, altitude, and speed to air traffic control and other aircraft.

ADS-B In is the receiving side of the system. It allows aircraft to receive the same information transmitted by nearby aircraft and display it directly in the cockpit. With it, pilots gain a real-time picture of surrounding traffic, updated every second and extending up to 180 nautical miles away.

The technology gives crews GPS-level situational awareness that supports safer spacing, conflict avoidance, and more efficient traffic management.

Why ADS-B In matters

While ADS-B In is a safety technology, it can also improve operational efficiency. According to Acron Aviation, the system can enable more precise aircraft spacing, increase runway throughput, and reduce go-arounds. It also supports Interval Management procedures, which help aircraft maintain optimum separation while reducing fuel burn and emissions.

The FAA’s two-year evaluation of ACSS SafeRoute+ with American Airlines at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport showed these benefits in live operations.

“ADS-B In can be installed in as little as 1-2 shifts, so there’s no lengthy downtime for aircraft,” said Cam Morast, Product Manager at ACSS. “In addition, fleets equipped with the technology will see meaningful operational returns. The two-year FAA evaluation at Dallas-Fort Worth with American Airlines logged an average 12-second reduction in arrival spacing, equating to four to five extra landings per hour, per runway, with 490,000 lbs of fuel saved in the first year alone, and zero separation-related safety incidents.”

Airline ADS-B In equipment outpaces understanding

The survey of 100 US airline executives and managers conducted in April found that 47% said their airlines had already equipped some or all of their fleets with ADS-B In, while another 40% were evaluating the technology.

However, the understanding of the technology’s capabilities was far weaker.

One-third of respondents said they did not understand the difference between ADS-B In and ADS-B Out.

Just 61% were aware that ADS-B In provides pilots with traffic awareness out to 180 nautical miles.

Only 42% recognized its potential to reduce fuel burn and carbon emissions.

Only 37% were aware that the technology could reduce go-arounds.

The study concluded that many airlines may be making investment decisions without fully appreciating the operational and financial benefits.

Airlines believe they can comply with an ADS-B In mandate

Despite these knowledge gaps, 86% of respondents said they believed their airlines could comply with a mandate within three years.

Damien Moreau, president of Acron Aviation’s ACSS business, said the industry’s enthusiasm for the technology is clear, but education remains essential.

“The data shows the appetite for ADS-B In exists,” said Moreau. “This study also tells us that boardroom confidence is outpacing what’s actually understood about the technology at the decision-making level, so the industry needs to work to educate people on the real advantages it brings. The airlines that see the most benefits from ADS-B In will be the ones that treat it as an operational investment with measurable returns in fuel, capacity, and on-time performance.”

According to the report, 85% of airline executives believe carriers that equip early will gain a competitive advantage, while 88% expect ADS-B In to become mandatory eventually.

Although nearly nine out of ten respondents believe they are prepared for a mandate, Acron’s findings suggest the industry’s readiness may be less advanced in its potential applications.

The company also adopted NASA’s open-source Aviary multidisciplinary design and optimization tool and developed an electrified aircraft design suite intended for public use.

text:
Latest configuration could deliver up to a 17 percent efficiency

The technique is known as boundary layer ingestion. Electra’s analysis found that the configuration could deliver up to a 17 percent efficiency improvement beyond gains expected by 2050 from advanced structures, engine technologies, and aerodynamic improvements.

“The value of electrification in this concept is that it lets us put the propulsion where it couldn’t go before but does the most good,” said Dr. Parker Vascik, Director of Product Strategy at Electra.

“We can radically improve how the airframe and propulsion system work together while keeping the aircraft grounded in real airline and airport operations. The goal is not just efficiency on paper, but concepts that we can actually build, certify, and use.”

The company also revealed that the concept is designed to fit within existing airport gates and airline operations, use standard jet fuel or sustainable aviation fuel, and avoid reliance on airport charging infrastructure or untested fuel types. The configuration also supports a twin-aisle cabin layout within a narrowbody aircraft class, unlocking improved passenger comfort and more efficient boarding and deplaning.

The concept is developed as part of NASA’s Advanced Aircraft Concepts for Environmental Sustainability (AACES) 2050 program.

“This concept builds on years of research into how airframe shape and propulsion placement can work together to improve aircraft efficiency,” said Dr. Alejandra Uranga, Electra’s Chief Engineer for Research and Future Concepts.

“What is different now is the ability to use electrification and distributed propulsion to more deeply integrate those systems. Designing the aircraft as a whole system is essential to realizing the full potential of future commercial aircraft.”

NASA’s open-source Aviary multidisciplinary design adopted

In addition to the concept, Electra developed 11 technical papers documenting the models, methods, and findings behind the study. The company also adopted NASA’s open-source Aviary multidisciplinary design and optimization tool and developed an electrified aircraft design suite intended for public use. Together, these contributions are intended to help advance the broader aviation research community, not just push forward a single aircraft concept, according to a press release.

Electra’s AACES 2050 team brought together leaders across industry and academia, including American Airlines, Honeywell Aerospace, Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, Hinetics, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, the University of Michigan Department of Aerospace Engineering, and the University of California, Irvine’s Aircraft Systems Laboratory, as per the release.

“Through AACES, NASA is pushing the industry to think boldly, to use our novel propulsion technologies to unconstrain design thinking for the next generation of commercial aviation,” said Marc Allen, CEO of Electra.

“The third era of aviation will bring radical change to how people and places connect, whether applied to aircraft entering service this decade, future regional platforms, or commercial transport by mid-century. Electra’s focus as the hybrid electric leader is to keep American aviation, and NASA, leading the way.”
